1 Toolbox for proving lower bounds

The lower bound does not rely on a specific strategy. But it tells us why we cannot do better. This impossibility always stems from the fact that the lack of information.

In this chapter, we first discuss the necessary information to distinguish between two distributions. Many algorithms for complex problems have been proved to violate this lower bound, thus proving a no-go theorem for reaching the lower bound.

1.1 Le-Cam’s bound

We first upper bound the ability to distinguish two classical distributions p and q, as shown in Lemma [lemma:TV_bound] below.

重要Lemma

If two distributions p,q on set S = \{1,\cdots,n\} has total variance distance (TVD) \|p - q\|_{\mathrm {TV}}:=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i = 1}^n|p(i) - q(i)| \leq \varepsilon, then there is no single sample algorithm \mathcal{A}: S \to \{p,q\} that \varepsilon/2 better than random guessing, in other words, satisfied \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] \geq 1/2 + \varepsilon/2 and \text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = q] \geq 1/2 + \varepsilon/2.

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. It is sufficient to show that for an arbitrary algorithm \mathcal{A}, either \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = q] \geq (1-\varepsilon)/2 or \text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] \geq (1-\varepsilon)/2. Notice that \begin{align} \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = q] + \text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] & = 1 - \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] +\text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p]\\ &\geq 1 - \sup_{U \subseteq S} \left |\text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[U] -\text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[U]\right |\\ &= 1 - \|p - q\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \geq 1 - \varepsilon. \end{align} Then either \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = q] \geq (1-\varepsilon)/2 or \text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] \geq (1-\varepsilon)/2, which means that either \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] \leq (1+\varepsilon)/2 or \text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] \leq (1+\varepsilon)/2. ◻

A slight generalization of Lemma [lemma:TV_bound] is to distinguish a unique distribution p_0 and multiple distributions p_1,\cdots,p_l for L =\{1,\cdots,l\}, where p_i are all distributions over set S=\{1,\cdots,n\}. We prove a generalized no-go theorem below:

重要Lemma

If there exists a distribution \mathcal{D} over L such that \delta_{\mathcal{D}}:=\|p_0 - \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}]\|_{\mathrm {TV}} \leq \varepsilon, then there is no single-sampling algorithm that distinguishes p_0 between p_1,\cdots,p_l such that it is \varepsilon/2 better than random guessing.

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. We first directly prove this result using lemma [lemma:TV_bound]. If it exists, we can use it as an algorithm that distinguishes the distribution q(i):=\mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}(i)] with p_0(i) and it is \varepsilon/2 better than random guessing. This contradicts the fact that \|p_0 - q\|_{\mathrm {TV}} =\|p_0 - \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}]\|_{\mathrm {TV}} \leq \varepsilon according to Lemma [lemma:TV_bound]. ◻

In Lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound], we can try all kinds of distribution \mathcal{D} over L and choose the hardest one \delta_{\mathrm{w}} = \min_{\mathcal{D}}\delta_{\mathcal{D}}. This reflects the worst case information complexity of this discrimination problem.

1.1.1 Problem ensemble and average case hardness.

In general, this problem is much harder than two-point discrimination, as we are designing a unified algorithm that dealt with multiple two-point discrimination (p_0,p_1),\cdots,(p_0,p_L) at the same time. One can relax this problem by ensuring that the distribution p_i only appears following a fixed distribution \mathcal{D}. This reduces the problem to a two-point discrimination (p_0,\mathbb{E}_{r \sim \mathcal{D}}p_r). Then the value \delta_{\mathcal{D}} in Lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound] is tight. We call it the average case information complexity under problem ensemble \mathcal{D}. Similarly, we can define multiple-to-multiple tasks that discriminate a set of distribution \mathcal{A} from the other set of distribution \mathcal{B}, whose average case hardness is defined by \|\mathbb{E}_{r \sim \mathcal{D}(A)}p_{r} -\mathbb{E}_{r \sim \mathcal{D}(B)} q_{s}\|_{\mathrm{TVD}} for problem ensemble \mathcal{D}(\mathcal A) and \mathcal{D}(\mathcal B).

1.1.2 Replica tells ensemble from its average.

One confusing point is the discrimination of the distribution p_0 = \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}] and a set of distribution \{p_{r}\} with problem ensemble {r \sim \mathcal{D}}. By Lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound], we cannot distinguish them with probability greater than 1/2 given one-sample. However, under k-samples, this is equivalent to the discrimination of p_0(t_1)\cdots p_0(t_k) and a set of distribution \{p_{r}(t_1)\cdots p_{r}(t_k)\} with problem ensemble {r \sim \mathcal{D}}. We can check that \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}} \left[p_{r}(t_1)\cdots p_{r}(t_k)\right] \neq p_0(t_1)\cdots p_0(t_k) \\ = \left[\mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}p_{r}(t_1)\right]\cdots \left[\mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}p_{r}(t_k)\right], thus can be estimated with probability greater than 1/2.

1.1.3 Coarse graining.

Intuitively, distinguishing two fine-grained distributions is never more difficult than distinguishing their coarse-grained versions. With TVD, we quantify this intuition as Lemma [lemma:TVD_corse].

重要Lemma

Given two distribution \mathbf{p}:=\{p_1,\cdots,p_M\},\mathbf{q}:=\{q_1,\cdots,q_M\} and their coarse graining \mathbf{P}:=\bigcup_{s}\{p_{1,s},\cdots,p_{M,s}\},\mathbf{Q}:=\bigcup_{s}\{q_{1,s},\cdots,q_{M,s}\} such that \sum_{s} p_{k,s} = p_k,\sum_{s} q_{k,s} = q_k, \forall k \in \{1,\cdots,M\}. Then \|\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{Q}\|_{\mathrm{tvd}} \geq \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}\|_{\mathrm{tvd}}.

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. Since \|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{tvd}} = 2^{-1}\|\cdot\|_{1}, we conclude that \|\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{Q}\|_{1} = \sum_{k,s}\|p_{k,s} - q_{k,s}\|_{1} \geq \sum_{k}\|\sum_{s}p_{k,s} - \sum_{s}q_{k,s}\|_{1} = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}\|_{1} ◻

The most general form of the lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound] is Le Cam’s bound. We prove this theorem and show that lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound] is a special case of the Le-Cam theorem [theo:Le_Cam] for completeness.

重要Theorem

Given a measurable space x \in \mathcal{X} and a family of measures P \in \mathcal{P}, P: 2^\mathcal{X} \to [0,1]. Let \hat \theta:\mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}^p be an arbitrary estimator of the parameters of this family of distributions \theta: \mathcal{P} \to \mathbb{R}^p. Let D[\cdot,\cdot]:\mathbb{R}^p \times \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be a pseudo-metric of the parameter space that is symmetric and satisfies the triangular inequality D(x,y)+D(y,z) \geq D(x,z). Take two arbitrary subsets \mathcal{P}_1, \mathcal{P}_2 \subset \mathcal{P} that satisfied \inf_{\substack{P_1 \in \mathcal{P}_1,P_2 \in \mathcal{P_2}} } D\left[\theta(P_1), \theta(P_2)\right] \geq 2\delta, then the inequality is true: \begin{align} \sup_{P \in \mathcal{P}} \left[\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} dP(x)\cdot D\left[\hat \theta(x),\theta(P)\right]\right] \\ &\geq \delta\cdot \sup_{\substack{P_1 \in \text{cov~}\mathcal{P}_1\\P_2 \in \text{cov~} \mathcal{P_2}} } \left[1 - \frac{1}{2}\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} [dP_1(x) - dP_2(x)]\right]. \end{align}

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. We first noted that \begin{align} 2\sup_{P \in \mathcal{P}} \left[\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} dP(x)\cdot D\left[\hat\theta(x),\theta(P)\right]\right] \\ &\geq \int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} dP_1(x)\cdot D\left[\hat\theta(x),\theta(P_1)\right] \\ &\quad + \int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} dP_2(x)\cdot D\left[\hat\theta(x),\theta(P_2)\right]. \end{align} Based on the triangular inequality, we have D\left[\hat\theta(x),\theta(P_1)\right] + D\left[\hat\theta(x),\theta(P_2)\right] \geq D\left[\theta(P_1),\theta(P_2)\right]\geq 2\delta. Thus, for a fixed point x, the tuple (f_1/2\delta,f_2/2\delta), \text{where }\begin{cases}f_1(x) =D[ \hat \theta(x),\theta(P_1)], \\f_2(x) =D[ \hat \theta(x),\theta(P_2)],\end{cases} is in the convex set \mathcal{S} =\{(r_1,r_2)\in \mathbb{R}^2| r_1,r_2\geq 0,r_1+r_2 \geq 1\}. Then \forall P_1 \in \mathcal{P}_1,\forall P_2 \in \mathcal{P}_2, we write the inequality \begin{align} 2\sup_{P \in \mathcal{P}} \left[\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} dP(x)\cdot D\left[\hat\theta(x),\theta(P)\right]\right] \\ &\geq 2\delta\cdot \left[\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \inf_{[r_1(x),r_2(x)] \in \mathcal{S}} \left[dP_1(x)\cdot r_1(x) + dP_2(x)\cdot r_2(x)\right]\right]\\ &\geq \sup_{\substack{P_1 \in \text{cov~}\mathcal{P}_1\\P_2 \in \text{cov~} \mathcal{P_2}} } 2\delta\cdot \\ &\quad \left[\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \inf_{[r_1(x),r_2(x)] \in \mathcal{S}} \left[dP_1(x)\cdot r_1(x) + dP_2(x)\cdot r_2(x)\right]\right]. \end{align} The RHS satisfied the identity \begin{align} \text{RHS} &=2\delta \sup_{\substack{P_1 \in \text{cov~}\mathcal{P}_1\\P_2 \in \text{cov~} \mathcal{P_2}} } \\ &\quad \left[\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \inf_{ \substack{r_1(x),r_2(x)\geq 0,\\r_1(x)+r_2(x) = 1}} \left[dP_1(x)\cdot r_1(x) +dP_2(x)\cdot r_2(x)\right]\right]\\ &=2\delta \sup_{\substack{P_1 \in \text{cov~}\mathcal{P}_1\\P_2 \in \text{cov~} \mathcal{P_2}} } \\ &\quad \left[1 +\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \inf_{ r_1(x)\in [0, 1]}\left[dP_1(x)\cdot r_1(x) - dP_2(x)\cdot r_1(x)\right]\right]\\ &=2\delta \sup_{\substack{P_1 \in \text{cov~}\mathcal{P}_1\\P_2 \in \text{cov~} \mathcal{P_2}} } \\ &\quad \left[1- \int_{\substack{x \in \mathcal{X}\\P_2(x) \geq P_1(x)}} dP_2(x) - dP_1(x) \right]\\ &=2\delta \sup_{\substack{P_1 \in \text{cov~}\mathcal{P}_1\\P_2 \in \text{cov~} \mathcal{P_2}} } \\ &\quad \left[1- \frac{1}{2} \int_{\substack{x \in \mathcal{X}}} |dP_2(x) - dP_1(x)| \right]. \end{align} This completes the proof. ◻

重要Lemma

The lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound] is a special case of the Le-Cam theorem [theo:Le_Cam].

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. Take the special case that \mathcal{X} = \{1,\cdots,n\}, \mathcal{P}_0 =\{p_0(x)\}, \mathcal{P}_1 =\{p_1(x),\cdots,p_l(x)\} and \theta(p_i) :=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }i =0,\\1&\text{else}.\end{cases} The estimator and metric are taken as \hat \theta(\cdot): \mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\} and \begin{align} D(\cdot,\cdot): \{0,1\}^{2} \to \{0,1\}, \\ (\theta_1,\theta_2) &\hookrightarrow \begin{cases}1&\text{if }(\theta_1,\theta_2)=(1,0),(0,1),\\ 0 &\text{else}.\end{cases} \end{align} It is easy to see that D(\cdot,\cdot) is indeed symmetric and satisfies the triangular inequality. This strategy distinguished the \mathcal{P}_0 and \mathcal{P}_1 with success probability \begin{align} p_{\text{succ}} &=\min_{i=1,\cdots,l}\left\{ \text{Pr}_{x \sim p_0}[\hat \theta(x) =0 ],\text{Pr}_{x \sim p_i}[\hat \theta(x) =1 ]\right\} \\ &= 1 - \max_{i = 1,\cdots,l}\left\{ \text{Pr}_{x \sim p_0}[\hat \theta(x) =1 ],\text{Pr}_{x \sim p_i}[\hat \theta(x) =0 ]\right\}\\ &=1 - \max_{p \in \mathcal{P}} E_{x \sim p} D[\hat \theta(x),\theta(p)]. \end{align} Based on Lemma [theo:Le_Cam], we conclude the inequality \begin{align} \max_{p \in \mathcal{P}} E_{x \sim p} D[\hat \theta(x),\theta(p)] \geq \delta\cdot [1 - \|p_0 - \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}]\|_{\mathrm {TV}} ]. \end{align} Notice that \inf_{\substack{P_1 \in \mathcal{P}_1,P_2 \in \mathcal{P_2}} } D\left[\theta(P_1), \theta(P_2)\right] \geq 1, we take \delta = 1/2, which combine to the final result \begin{align} p_{\text{succ}} \leq 1 -\frac{1 - \|p_0 - \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}]\|_{\mathrm {TV}} }{2} = \frac{1 + \|p_0 - \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}]\|_{\mathrm {TV}} }{2} . \end{align} Then if \|p_0 - \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}]\|_{\mathrm {TV}} \leq \varepsilon, we conclude that p_{\text{succ}}\leq (1+\varepsilon)/2 and cannot \varepsilon/2 better than random guessing. ◻

1.2 Restriction on POVMs

Now we specify different POVM restrain \mathcal{M} = \{\{F_s\}|\{F_s\} \text{~satisfied the restriction.}\}. In general, we can keep c copies of identical state \rho^{\otimes c}, and implement a c-replica measurement. Such a strategy are specified by as set of POVM operators \{F_s \in \mathrm{Herm}(d^c)\}_{s \in \mathcal{S}}, with s \in \mathcal{S} specified the measurement results and \forall s \in \mathcal{S}, F_s \geq 0, \sum_s {F_s} = \mathbb{I}(d)^{\otimes c}. We first show that we can always restrain the form of \{F_{s}\}_{s} on rank-1 operator set \{w_{s}\ket{\psi_{s}}\!\bra{\psi_{s}}\}_{s} without loss of generality. This is because arbitrary POVMs can be simulated by rank-1 POVMs through grouping the results.

重要Lemma

Any POVM \{F_s\}_s can be simulated through rank-1 POVM \{w_{sp}\cdot\ket{\psi_{sp}}\!\bra{\psi_{sp}}\}_{sp} by classical post-grouping \ket{\psi_{sp}}\!\bra{\psi_{sp}} \to F_s.

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. Do Cholesky decomposition. Trivial. ◻

This equivalence means that given an arbitrary state \rho, the classical distribution generated by \{w_{sp}\cdot\ket{\psi_{sp}}\!\bra{\psi_{sp}}\}_{sp} is a coarse graining of that of \{F_s\}_s. Using Lemma [lemma:TVD_corse], we conclude that it is sufficient to consider rank-1 POVMs only.

Based on different experiment restriction, F_s might only supports on a subset of space \mathrm{Herm}(d^c). Here below we characterized some typical restriction.

1.2.1 Restriction on the memory

We first focus on the k-memory c-replica strategies. It is a c-replica measurement but with finite quantum-storage, as formally defined below.

注记Definition

A (c,k) adaptive strategy repeats T rounds of sampling. Within each round, as shown in the process diagram [eq:procc_diag], it repeatedly adds new copies of n-qubits \rho to the k-qubits memory \sigma^{(i)} and adaptively implements n+k \to k qubits POVMs \{M_s^{u}\}. \begin{align} \label{eq:procc_diag} \left[\rho \xrightarrow{\{M_{s_1}\}} \sigma^{(1)} \xrightarrow{\text{Add } \rho} \rho \otimes \sigma^{(1)}\xrightarrow{\{M_{s_1,s_2}\}} \sigma^{(2)} \xrightarrow{\text{Add } \rho} \cdots \rho \otimes \sigma^{(c)}\xrightarrow{\{M_{s_1,\cdots,s_c}\}} R_r \right]_{\times T} \end{align}

At the end of each round in a (c,k)-adaptive strategy, we get the result s_1,s_2,\cdots,s_c, corresponding to the POVM branch \begin{aligned} &\{M_{s_1}:\mathrm{Lin}(\mathcal{H}(d^{n}),\mathcal{H}(d^{k_1})), \\ &\quad M_{s_1,s_2}:\mathrm{Lin}(\mathcal{H}(d^{n + k_1}),\mathcal{H}(d^{k_2})), \cdots, \\ &\quad M_{s_1,s_2,\cdots,s_c}:\mathrm{Lin}(\mathcal{H}(d^{n + k_{c-1}}), \mathbb{C})\}. \end{aligned} Here the parameter satisifed k_1 = \min\{n,k\}, k_2 = \min\{n+k_1,k\},\cdots,k_{c-1} = \min\{n+k_{c-2},k\}. The POVM operator \{F_{\mathbf{s}}\} belongs to the linear space \mathrm{Lin}(\mathcal{H}(d^{cn})). When k = (c-1)\cdot n, we have k_1 = n,k_2 = 2n,\cdots,k_{c-1} = (c-1)n. This means that the last POVM operator supports on the whole linear space M_{s_1,s_2,\cdots,s_c}:\mathrm{Lin}(\mathcal{H}(d^{cn}), \mathbb{C}). Thus, the round-POVM operators \{F_s\} cover the whole space \mathrm{Lin}(\mathcal{H}(d^{cn})) and are equivalent to first storing c-copies of n-qudit states followed by c-copies collective measurements. If k < (c-1)n, \{F_s\} is restricted which we denoted as the set \mathcal{M}_{c,n}^{k}. We show that every element of \mathcal{M}_{c,n}^{k} can be realized by rank-1 POVMs within \mathcal{M}_{c,n}^{k} and post coarse-graining of the measurement results. Thus, it is sufficient to lower bounding all the rank-1 \mathcal{M}_{c,n}^{k} POVMs \mathcal{M}_{c,n}^k = \{F_{j}:= 2^{cn}w_j|L_j\rangle\!\langle L_j|\}_{j}, with \sum_{j}F_j = \mathbb{I}(d^{cn}).

重要Lemma

\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}_{c,n}^{k} has decomposition \{F_s:= d^{nc}\sum_{a_c}w_{s,a_c}|L_{s,a_c}\rangle\!\langle L_{s,a_c}|\}_s, where \ket{L_{s,a_c}} is a normalized MPS vector on c \cdot n qudits with at most d^{k_j} bond dimension.

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. The operator F_s can be constructed from those M_s operators through the identity: \begin{align} \mathrm{tr}(\rho^{\otimes c} F_s) = \sum_{a_c \in [d^{n+k}]}\begin{quantikz}[row sep=0.1cm, column sep=0.1cm] \setwiretype{n}&&&\gate[2]{M_{s_1, s_2}}&\gate[1]{M_{s_1}\vphantom{M_{s_1}^\dagger}}\setwiretype{c}&\gate[1]{\rho}\setwiretype{q}&\gate[1]{M_{s_1}^\dagger}\gategroup[4,steps=6,style={dashed,rounded corners,inner sep=-1pt},label style={label position=below, yshift=0.65cm, xshift=-0.7cm}]{$\ket{L_{s,a_c}}$}&\gate[2]{M_{s_1, s_2}^\dagger}\setwiretype{c}\\ \setwiretype{n}&&\gate[2]{\cdots}\setwiretype{n}&\setwiretype{c}&\setwiretype{q}&\gate[1]{\rho}&&&\gate[2]{\cdots}\setwiretype{c}\\ \setwiretype{n}&\gate[2]{M_{s_1,\cdots,s_c}}&\setwiretype{c}&\setwiretype{q}&&\gate[1]{\cdot\!\!\cdot\!\!\cdot}&&&&\gate[2]{M_{s_1,\cdots,s_c}^\dagger}\setwiretype{c}\\ \lstick{$a_c$|\!|\!\!\!}\setwiretype{c}&&\setwiretype{q}&&&\gate[1]{\rho}&&&&&\setwiretype{c}&\rstick{\!\!\!|\!|$a_c$} \end{quantikz} \label{eq:tensor_network_MPS} \end{align} Here we use single line to indicate the d-dimensional bond and double line to indicate the k_j-dimensional bond. The restriction of such (c,k)-POVM operators, which we denoted as the set \mathcal{M}_{c,n}^{k}, is equivalent to state that \{F_s:= d^{nc}\sum_{a_c}w_{s,a_c}|L_{s,a_c}\rangle\!\langle L_{s,a_c}|\}_s with \ket{L_{s,a_c}} a normalized MPS vector on c \cdot n qudits with d^{k_j} bond dimension: \begin{align} &\ket{L_{s,a_c}} =\sum_{a_j\in [d^{k_j}]} \ket{L_{s,a_1}}\ket{L_{s,a_1,a_2}}\cdots \ket{L_{s,a_{c-2},a_{c-1}}}\ket{L_{s,a_{c-1},a_c}}, \text{~where~} \forall \ket{e} \in \mathcal{H}(d^n),\\ &\langle e|{L_{s,a_1}}\rangle := \langle e|M_{s_1}^{\dagger}|a_1\rangle,\quad \langle e|{L_{s,a_{j-1},a_{j}}}\rangle := \langle e,a_{j-1}|M_{s_1,\cdots,s_j}^{\dagger}|a_{j}\rangle,\forall j>1. \end{align} The trace-preserving condition \sum_{s_j} M^{\dagger}_{s_1,\cdots,s_j}M_{s_1,\cdots,s_j} = \mathbb{I}(d^n) now transformed into \begin{align} \sum_{a_j,s_j} \langle e|{L_{s,a_{j-1},a_{j}}}\rangle \langle {L_{s,a_{j-1},a_{j}}}|f\rangle &= \sum_{a_j}\langle e,a_{j-1}|M_{s_1,\cdots,s_j}^{\dagger}|a_{j}\rangle\langle a_{j}|M_{s_1,\cdots,s_j}|f,a_{j-1}\rangle\\ &=\sum_{s_j}\langle e,a_{j-1}|M_{s_1,\cdots,s_j}^{\dagger}M_{s_1,\cdots,s_j}|f,a_{j-1}\rangle = \delta_{e,f} \\ &\hspace{-5em}\Rightarrow \forall j = 1,\cdots,c,\quad \sum_{a_j,s_j} |{L_{s,a_{j-1},a_{j}}}\rangle \langle {L_{s,a_{j-1},a_{j}}}|= \mathbb{I}(d^n). \end{align} Thus, \mathcal{M}_{c,n}^k can be implemented through rank-1 MPS-POVMs \mathcal{M}_{c,n}^k = \{F_{j}:= 2^{cn}w_j|L_j\rangle\!\langle L_j|\}_{j=(s,a_c)}, with \sum_{j}F_j = \mathbb{I}(d^{cn}), followed by classical post-processing rule j=(s,a_c) \to s. ◻

Given a pure quantum state \ket{L} that supports on c identical quantum systems with subsystem S \subset \{1,\cdots,c\}. Define P^S as the tensor product of Pauli operator P on the subsystem s if s \in S otherwise identity. We say the Pauli operator P are \varepsilon-correlated on the subsystem if and only if |\bra{L} P^{S} \ket{L}|^2 \geq \varepsilon. For a 2^k-bonded MPS states \ket{L}, we show that the \varepsilon-correlated Pauli is only taking no more than \varepsilon^{-1}2^{-n + k} proportion within all possible Pauli operators, as rigorously stated in Lemma [lemma:MPS_Paulicorrelation].

重要Lemma

Define the average Pauli correlation on subsystem S \subset \{1,\cdots,c\} as \mathcal{P}(S):= 4^{-n}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} |\bra{L} P^{\otimes S} \ket{L}|^2. Then if \ket{L} is an MPS state with no more than 2^k bond dimension, we have \mathcal{P}(S) \leq 2^{-n + k}. In the special case |S| = 1, \mathcal{P}(S) \leq 2^{-n}.

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. In the simplest case c = 2,d= 2, a MPS state with \leq 2^k bond dimension always has Schmidt decomposition \ket{L} = \sum_{a = 1}^{2^k} \sqrt{\lambda_a} \ket{\phi_a} \otimes \ket{\psi_a} with \sum_a \lambda_a = 1. Take P^{\{1,2\}} = P \otimes P,P^{\{1\}} = P \otimes \mathbb{I}_n, then \begin{align} \mathcal{P}(\{1,2\}) &= 2^{-2n}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} \left|\sum_{a,a'}\sqrt{\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}}\bra{\phi_a}P\ket{\phi_{a'}}\bra{\psi_a}P \ket{\psi_{a'}}\right|^2\notag\\ &\leq 2^{-2n}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} \left( \sum_{a,a'}\left|\sqrt{\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}}\bra{\phi_a}P\ket{\phi_{a'}}\right|^2\right)\cdot \left(\sum_{a,a'}\left|\bra{\psi_a}P \ket{\psi_{a'}}\right|^2\right) \notag\\ &\leq 2^{-2n + k}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} \sum_{a,a'}\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}\left|\bra{\phi_a}P\ket{\phi_{a'}}\right|^2 = 2^{-n + k} \sum_{a,a'}\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}\bra{\phi_a\phi_{a'}}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} 2^{-n}P \otimes P\ket{\phi_{a'}\phi_a}\notag\\ &=2^{-n + k} \sum_{a,a'}\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}\bra{\phi_a\phi_{a'}}\ket{\phi_{a}\phi_{a'}} =2^{-n + k},\\ \mathcal{P}(\{1\}) &= 2^{-2n}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} \left|\sum_{a,a'}\sqrt{\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}}\bra{\phi_a}P\ket{\phi_{a'}}\bra{\psi_a}\ket{\psi_{a'}}\right|^2 = 2^{-2n}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} \left|\sum_{a}{\lambda_a}\bra{\phi_a}P\ket{\phi_{a}}\right|^2 \notag\\ &=2^{-n} \sum_{a}{\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}}\bra{\phi_a\phi_{a'}}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} 2^{-n}P \otimes P\ket{\phi_{a}\phi_{a'}}= 2^{-n} \sum_{a}{\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}}\bra{\phi_a\phi_{a'}}\ket{\phi_{a'}\phi_{a}}\leq 2^{-n}. \end{align} This generalized to c>2 case by noticing that \ket{L} = \sum_{a = 1}^{2^k} \sqrt{\lambda_a} \ket{\phi_a} \otimes \ket{\psi_a} is satisfied for bipartition \{1,\cdots,l\} \cup \{l+1,c\}. Take l being the least on in set S. For special case |S| = 1, it is trivially the same as c = 2 case. For |S| \geq 2, the same procedure followed: \begin{align} \mathcal{P}(S) &= 2^{-2n}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} \left|\sum_{a,a'}\sqrt{\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}}\bra{\phi_a}P^{\{l\}}\ket{\phi_{a'}}\bra{\psi_a}P^{S - \{l\}} \ket{\psi_{a'}}\right|^2\leq 2^{-2n + k}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} \sum_{a,a'}\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}\left|\bra{\phi_a}P^{\{l\}}\ket{\phi_{a'}}\right|^2 \notag \\ &= 2^{-n + k} \sum_{a,a'}\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}\bra{\phi_a\phi_{a'}}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} 2^{-n}P^{\{l\}} \otimes P^{\{l\}}\ket{\phi_{a'}\phi_a}\leq 2^{-n + k} \sum_{a,a'}\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}=2^{-n + k}. \end{align} ◻

In the case of c =2, we also have the inequality below:

重要Lemma

\begin{align} \max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}^{k}_{2,n}} \sum_{s} \frac{\left[\mathrm{tr}(F_s \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n})\right]^2}{\mathrm{tr}(F_s)} \leq 2^{k+n} \end{align}

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. ◻

1.2.2 Restriction on the locality

1.2.3 Restriction on the magic

1.3 Tree representation of adaptive strategy

Given an implementable POVM set \mathcal{M} = \{\{F_s\}|\{F_s\} \text{~satisfied the restriction.}\}, we can implement those POVMs multiple times, carefully design their order, and even implement them adaptively. Any description of such an adaptive learning protocol are called a \mathcal{M}-restrained adaptive strategy. It has the Tree representation  [1]. Roughly speaking, the adaptive structure will first induce a decision tree \mathcal{T}. Each branching edges in \mathcal{T}, which we denoted as \{(u,v_1),\cdots,(u,v_{s_u})\}, was labeled by one of the restrained POVMs \{F^{u}_{v_{i}}\}_{i = 1}^{s_u} \in \mathcal{M}. Then any c-copies of state \rho \in \mathcal{H}(d^c) will induce a probability distribution p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(v) on each vertex v of the decision graph \mathcal{T}.

注记Definition

Consider an adaptive learning strategy with T-rounds of c-replica POVMs restrained on \mathcal{M}. The tree representation of it is

  • A T-level decision tree \mathcal{T} with root node r.

  • Edges between node u and its child nodes s_1,\cdots,s_{N_u} represents a POVM \{F^{u}_s\}_{s =1}^{N_u} \in \mathcal{M} with the measurement outcomes \{1,\cdots,N_u\}.

  • Each node u is assigned a probability p_{\mathcal{T},\rho}(u) based on the updating rule p_{\rho}(u) = p_{\rho}(u|s)p_{\rho}(s), where p_{\rho}(s|u) = \text{tr}(F^u_{s} \rho) and p_{\rho}(r) = 1.

To prove that any \mathcal{M}-restrained adaptive strategy \mathcal{T} cannot distinguish the states \rho from a set of state \mathcal{S} with 1/2 + \varepsilon successful rate, it is sufficient to show that \forall \mathcal{T}, the distribution p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(l) and the distribution ensemble \{p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}(l)\}_{\sigma \in \mathcal{E}} cannot be distinguished \varepsilon/2 better than random guessing. This recasts the problem in a form that is solvable by applying Lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound]. Thus, the distinguishability between \rho and \mathcal{S} is tightly lower-bounded by TVD as \begin{align} \label{eq:tvd} \delta_{\mathrm{tvd}} :=\max_{\mathcal{T}}\min_{\mathcal{E}}\|p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}-\mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim\mathcal{E}} p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}, \end{align} where \mathcal{E} is an arbitrary distribution on the set \mathcal{S}. The analysis of \delta_{\mathrm{tvd}} requires brute-force calculation of leaves distribution p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(l),\mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim\mathcal{E}} p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}(l) on a deep decision tree. We can eschew this by constructing upper-bounds for TVD using the Leaves Likelihood L(l) and the Edges Likelihood L(u,s) of the decision tree. \begin{align} L_{\sigma}(l) := \frac{p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}(l)}{p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(l)} ,\quad L_{\sigma}(u,s):= \frac{p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}(s|u)}{p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(s|u)}. \end{align}

重要Lemma

Given distribution p^{(0)}(l) and distribution ensemble p^{(a)}(l),a \sim \mathcal{E} with L_a(l):=p^{(a)}(l)/p^{(0)}(l), then for any \beta \in (0,1), the TVD satisfied \begin{align} \|p^{(0)}-\mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \leq 1 - \min_{l}\mathbb{E}_a L_a(l), \quad \|p^{(0)}-\mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \leq \text{Pr}_{a\sim \mathcal{E},l \sim p^{(0)}}[L_a(l) \leq \beta] + (1 - \beta) \end{align}

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. By definition, we have \begin{align} \|p^{(0)}-\mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} &:= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{l \in \text{leaf}} |p^{(0)}(l) - \mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}(l)| = \sum_{l \in \text{leaf}} p^{(0)}(l)\cdot \max\{0, 1 -\mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}(l)/p^{(0)}(l)\}\\ &\leq \mathbb{E}_a \sum_{l \in \text{leaf}} p^{(0)}(l)\cdot \max\{0, 1 -p^{(a)}(l)/p^{(0)}(l)\}\\ &=\left[\sum_{\substack{a,l \in \text{leaf}\\\text{~s.t.~}L_a(l)\leq \beta}}p^{(0)}(l)\cdot \max \{0,1 - L_a(l)\}+\sum_{\substack{a,l \in \text{leaf}\\\text{~s.t.~}L_a(l)>\beta}}p^{(0)}(l)\cdot \max \{0,1 - L_a(l)\}\right]. \end{align} Here in the first line, we directly get the first inequality because \begin{align} \sum_{l \in \text{leaf}} p^{(0)}(l)\cdot \max\{0, 1 -\mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}(l)/p^{(0)}(l)\} \leq \sum_{l \in \text{leaf}} p^{(0)}(l)\cdot \left( 1 - \min_{l}\mathbb{E}_a L_a(l) \right) = 1 - \min_{l}\mathbb{E}_a L_a(l). \end{align} In the second line, we use the fact that \max \{0, 1- x\} is a convex function, thus f(\mathbb{E}_a x_a) \leq \mathbb{E}_a f(x_a). Because for any \beta \in (0,1), we have \begin{cases} \max\{0, 1 - L_a(l)\} \leq 1 - \beta, &\text{for } l \text{ s.t. } L_a(l) > \beta,\\ \max\{0, 1 - L_a(l)\} \leq 1, &\text{for } l \text{ s.t. } L_a(l) \leq \beta, \end{cases}, we obtain \begin{align} \|p^{(0)}-\mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} &\leq \sum_{\substack{a,l \in \text{leaf}\\L_a(l)\leq \beta}} p^{(0)}(l) + (1 - \beta) \sum_{\substack{a,l \in \text{leaf}\\L_a(l)> \beta}} p^{(0)}(l)\\ &= \text{Pr}_{a\sim \mathcal{E},l \sim p^{(0)}}[L_a(l) \leq \beta] +(1 - \beta)\cdot \text{Pr}_{a\sim \mathcal{E},l \sim p^{(0)}}[L_a(l) > \beta]\\ &\leq \text{Pr}_{a\sim \mathcal{E},l \sim p^{(0)}}[L_a(l) \leq \beta] + (1 - \beta). \end{align} ◻

Then we can simply prove that \forall l, \mathbb{E}_{\sigma\sim \mathcal{E}} L_{\sigma}(l) \geq 1 - \delta. Then use the first inequality in Lemma [lemma:UB_TVD], we have \|p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}-\mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim\mathcal{E}} p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \leq \delta. Or we can prove a fine-tuned upper bound for the probability \text{Pr}_{\sigma\sim \mathcal{E}, l \sim p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(l)}[L_{\sigma}(l) \leq \beta]. This is found by the proportion of Edges Likelihood L_{\sigma}(u,s), as illustrated by the inequality in the Lemma [lemma:UB_Ltail].

重要Lemma

If \forall u satisfied \mathbb{E}_{a\sim \mathcal{E}}\mathbb{E}_{s \sim p^{(0)}(s|u)}[(L_{a}(u,s) - 1)^2] \leq \delta, then for every constant c_1 \in (0,1/3), c_2 >0, there exists a constant c_3>0 such that \begin{align} \mathrm{Pr}_{a\sim \mathcal{E}, l \sim p^{(0)}}[L_a(l) \leq 1 - c_1] \leq c_2+ c_3\delta T. \end{align}

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. ◻

Now we are set to give a lower bound on Eq.[eq:tvd], which immediately lower bounding the measurement times T of the adaptive strategy \mathcal{T}, as shown in Theorem [theo:mart_distinguish_lb] blow:

重要Theorem

To distinguish \rho and a set of state \mathcal{S} for a constant success rate 1/2 + \varepsilon, with restrained POVMs \mathcal{M} and classical adaptive strategy, the adaptive measurement rounds T must be lower bounded by chi-squared divergence T > c \cdot \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\mathcal{S}}^{-1}, where \begin{align} \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\mathcal{S}} = \min_{\mathcal{E} \text{~on~} \mathcal{S}} \mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim \mathcal{E}} \max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}}\mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\sigma F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} - 1\right]^2. \end{align} Sometimes we use a loosing lower bound T > c \cdot \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\mathcal{S} \sim \mathcal{E}}^{-1} where \begin{align} \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\mathcal{S} \sim \mathcal{E}} := \max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}}\mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} \mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim \mathcal{E}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\sigma F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} - 1\right]^2. \end{align}

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. We first defined the likelihood function below: \begin{align} \label{eq:likelihood_func} \mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E},\rho) := \max_{u}\mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim \mathcal{E}} \mathbb{E}_{s \sim p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(s|u)} \left[\frac{p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}(s|u)}{p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(s|u)} - 1\right]^2 = \mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim \mathcal{E}} \max_{u}\mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s}^{u})} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\sigma F_{s}^{u})}{\mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s}^{u})} - 1\right]^2 \end{align} Combining Lemma [lemma:UB_TVD] and Lemma [lemma:UB_Ltail], this function upper-bounds the TVD through inequality \begin{align} \forall \mathcal{T},\mathcal{E},c_1 \in (0,1/3),c_2>0,&~\|p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}} - \mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim \mathcal{E}} p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \leq c_2 + c_3 \cdot \mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E},\rho) \cdot T + c_1,\\ \Rightarrow \forall c_1 \in (0,1/3),c_2>0,&~\delta_{\mathrm{tvd}} \leq c_2 + c_3 \cdot \max_{\mathcal{T}}\min_{\mathcal{E}}\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E},\rho) \cdot T + c_1. \end{align} Using Lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound], the correct probability 1/2 + \varepsilon to distinguish p_{\rho, \mathcal{T}} from \{p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}\}_{\sigma \in \mathcal{E}} must satisfy \begin{align} &1/2 + \varepsilon < 1/2 + \delta_{\mathrm{tvd}}/2 \leq 1/2+{(c_1+c_2)}/{2} + (1/2)c_3\cdot\max_{\mathcal{T}}\min_{\mathcal{E}}\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E},\rho)T\\ & \Rightarrow T > \frac{2 \varepsilon - c_1 -c_2}{c_3}\left[\max_{\mathcal{T}}\min_{\mathcal{E}}\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E},\rho)\right]^{-1} \geq c \cdot \left[\min_{\mathcal{E}}\max_{\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E},\rho)\right]^{-1}. \end{align} Here in the last inequality we use the max-min inequality \max_{\mathcal{T}}\min_{\mathcal{E}}\mathcal{F} \leq \min_{\mathcal{E}}\max_{\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{F}. As long as \varepsilon is a constant, we can always tune the value of c_1 \in (0,1/3),c_2>0 such that the lower bound T > c\cdot \max_{\mathcal{T}}\min_{\mathcal{E}}\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E}, \rho) is meaningful (i.e., c>0). Plug in the definition of \mathcal{F}, we get the equation T \geq c \cdot \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\mathcal{S}}^{-1}, where \begin{align} \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\mathcal{S}} = \min_{\mathcal{E}}\max_{\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E}, \rho) &=\min_{\mathcal{E}} \mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim \mathcal{E}} \max_{\mathcal{T}}\max_{u}\mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s}^{u})} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\sigma F_{s}^{u})}{\mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s}^{u})} - 1\right]^2 \\ &=\min_{\mathcal{E}} \mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim \mathcal{E}} \max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}}\mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\sigma F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} - 1\right]^2. \end{align} Here in the last line, we consider all possible adaptive strategy with POVM restriction \{F_s^{u}\} \in \mathcal{M}, \forall u, thus the maximum can be unioned. Sometimes we ignore the minimization over all possible ensemble \mathcal{E} over the state set \mathcal{S} and give a loose lower bound for the measurement times. We denoted this as: \begin{align} \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\mathcal{S}} \leq \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\mathcal{S} \sim \mathcal{E}} := \max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}}\mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} \mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim \mathcal{E}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\sigma F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} - 1\right]^2. \end{align} ◻

Before dived into complex prove of distinguishability lower bound, it is necessary to build an intuition about which ensemble is hard to distinguished.

重要Lemma

Given two state ensemble \mathcal{E}_1,\mathcal{E}_2. If \|\mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_1}[\rho^{\otimes k}] - \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_2}[\rho^{\otimes k}]\|_1 \\ := \|\mu^{(k)}_1 - \mu^{(k)}_2\|_{1}\geq \varepsilon, then there exists strategy that distinguishes \mathcal{E}_1 and \mathcal{E}_2 using k-replica measurement for O(1/\varepsilon^2) times.

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. Define function f(A):=\|A\|_1. Since f(A) is a closed and convex function, we conclude that f(A) = \max_{O}\left[\mathrm{tr}(O\cdot A) - f^*(O)\right]. The conjugate function writes: f^{*}(A) = \begin{cases}0 &\text{if~}\|A\|_{\infty}<1\\ +\infty &\text{if else}. \end{cases}, thus we have \|A\|_{1} = \max_{\|O\|_{\infty}<1}\mathrm{tr}(O\cdot A). Thus, the condition \|\mu^{(k)}_1 - \mu^{(k)}_2\|_{1}\geq \varepsilon is equivalent to the existence of O, \|O\|_{\infty}<1 such that \mathrm{tr}(O \mu^{(k)}_1) - \mathrm{tr}(O \mu^{(k)}_2) \geq \varepsilon. This means that we can measure operator O on k-replica state \rho^{\otimes k} and construct a direct estimator \hat{o} for \mathrm{tr}(O \mu^{(k)}). If the estimator \hat{o} has \leq \varepsilon/2 additive error, then it solves the discrimination problem. The condition O, \|O\|_{\infty}<1 means that -1<\mathrm{tr}(O \mu^{(k)}) < 1. We then can use Hoeffding inequality in Theorem [theo:Hoeff_inq] to bound the sampling complexity N < 2\varepsilon^{-2} \ln(2 \delta^{-1}) to constructing \hat{o} with \leq \varepsilon/2 additive error. ◻

For more general task to distinguish set S_1 form S_2, it is equivalent to build all possible distribution on S_1,S_2 and check the hardness of these constructed ensemble on S_1 and S_2. However, Lemma [lemma:hard_necess1] is only a necessary condition. Even if two ensembles have similar rank-k property, their might still exist efficient k-replica measurement strategy. An example is \mathbb{I}/d and \{\ket{\mathbf{s}}\!\bra{\mathbf{s}}\}_{\mathbf{s}} with \mathbf{s} uniformly distributed on \mathbb{F}_2^{n}. This is because although \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_1}[\rho^{\otimes k}] = \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_2}[\rho^{\otimes k}], we still have \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_1}[\prod_{i = 1}^{T}\mathrm{tr}(O_i\rho^{\otimes k})] \\ \neq \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_2}[\prod_{i = 1}^{T}\mathrm{tr}(O_i\rho^{\otimes k})].

With this intuition in mind, now we reviewed the information lower bound to distinguish Haar random state ensembles. Perhaps the most simple one are the maximum mixed state \mathbb{I}(d)/d with operator mixed ensemble.

1.4 Operator mixed ensemble and its distinguishability

Given access to either (i). A set of state {S}_{\mathcal{O}}:=\{(\mathbb{I}+ 3\varepsilon O_x)/d\}_{x \in \{1,\cdots,M\}} or (ii) \rho = \mathbb{I}/2^n, try to distinguish between these two cases with an error of at most 1/2-\varepsilon.

This problem determines the lower bound of classical shadow of \{O_x\}_{x \in \{1,\cdots,M\}} and has a special case for discrimination of \mathbb{I}/d and Pauli mixed state \rho = (\mathbb{I}+ 3\varepsilon P)/2^n with P \in \mathcal{P}_n.

We first get intuition of this task based on Lemma [lemma:hard_necess1]. If we choose distribution on \mathcal{O} supports on Z_1 operators only, we conclude that the value \|\mu_1^{(1)} - \mu_2^{(1)}\|_1 are separately \|3\varepsilon Z_1/2^n\|_1 = \mathrm{tr}\left({3\varepsilon \mathbb{I}/2^n}\right) = 3\varepsilon and \|4^{-n}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}}3\varepsilon P/2^n\|_1 \\ = 3\varepsilon \left[\mathrm{tr}\left(\sqrt{AA^\dagger}\right) \right]^{n} \\ = 3\varepsilon(\sqrt{3}/2)^n \sim \mathcal{O}(2^{-n}). Here we use \mathrm{tr}\left(\sqrt{AA^\dagger}\right) = \sum_{\lambda(A)}|\lambda(A)| and \begin{align} A = \frac{I+X+Y+Z}{4} =4^{-1} \begin{pmatrix}2&1- i\\1+i&0\end{pmatrix}, \quad \lambda(A) = {\frac{1 - \sqrt{3}}{4},\frac{1 + \sqrt{3}}{4}}. \end{align} This means that even though there exists easy distribution \mathrm{Pr}(P)=\delta(P - Z_1) on Pauli operators that can be distinguished with \mathbb{I}/d with single replica strategy, there also has distribution \mathrm{Pr}(P) = 4^{-n} that might be hard. Based on this intuition, we set up hard distributions as uniform distribution on signed operators \{+1,-1\}\times \mathcal{O}. This ensures its average is exactly \mathbb{I}/d, thus being hard for 1-replica strategy.

1.4.1 General operators

1.4.2 single-copy strategy.

For shadow tomography of general operator set \{O_1,\cdots,O_M\} where O_j is an arbitrary n-qubits operator, we build hard distribution by rotating Pauli Z operators with independent Haar random unitary: \begin{align} O_{1},\cdots,O_{M/2} &= U_1Z_1U_1^{\dagger}, \cdots, U_{M/2}Z_{M/2}U_{M/2}^{\dagger},\\ O_{M/2+1},\cdots,O_{M} &= -U_1Z_1U_1^{\dagger}, \cdots, -U_{M/2}Z_{M/2}U_{M/2}^{\dagger}, \end{align} where U_1,\cdots,U_{M/2} are independent Haar random unitaries. The signature is to ensure its average is \mathbb{I}/d such that Lemma [lemma:hard_necess1] cannot give effective single copy strategy. According to Lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound], to distinguish (i) and (ii) with 2/3 correction rate, which is \delta= 1/6 better that 1/2, we must have 1/3=2\delta \leq \|\mathbb{E}_{x} p_{\rho_x} - p_{2^{-n}\mathbb I}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}, where x is an arbitrary distribution on 1,\cdots,M. It is sufficient to take the uniform distribution of x. Based on Lemma [lemma:UB_TVD], 1/3\leq \|\mathbb{E}_{x} p_{\rho_x} - p_{2^{-n}\mathbb I}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \leq 1 - \min_{l} \mathbb{E}_{x} L_{x}(l). According to the rank-1 reduction in Lemma [lemma:POVM_r1_reduction], we calculate the leaves’ likelihood \forall l as \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{x} L_{x}(l) &= \frac{\mathbb{E}_{x} p_{\rho_x}(l)}{p_{2^{-n}\mathbb I}(l)} = \mathbb{E}_{x} \prod_{t = 1}^T \frac{w_{s_t}^{u_t}\bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}\rho_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}}{2^{-n}w_{s_t}^{u_t}}=\mathbb{E}_{x} \prod_{t = 1}^T \left(1+ 3\varepsilon\cdot \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}\right)\notag\\ &=\mathbb{E}_{x} \text{exp}\left[\sum_{t = 1}^T \ln\left(1+ 3\varepsilon\cdot \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}\right)\right]\geq \text{exp}\left[\sum_{t = 1}^T \mathbb{E}_{x} \ln\left(1+ 3\varepsilon\cdot \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}\right)\right]\notag\\ &=\text{exp}\left[\sum_{t = 1}^T M^{-1} \ln \left(\prod_{x = 1}^{M/2}\left(1+ 3\varepsilon\cdot \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}\right)\left(1- 3\varepsilon\cdot \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}\right)\right)\right]\notag\\ &=\text{exp}\left[\sum_{t = 1}^T M^{-1} \sum_{x = 1}^{M/2}\ln \left(1- 9\varepsilon^2\cdot \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}^2\right)\right] \notag\\ &\geq \text{exp}\left[-9\varepsilon^2\sum_{t = 1}^T \frac{2}{M}\sum_{x = 1}^{M/2} \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}^2\right] \geq \text{exp}\left[-9\varepsilon^2 T \sup_{\ket{\phi}}\frac{2}{M}\sum_{x = 1}^{M/2} \bra{\phi} O_x \ket{\phi}^2\right] \label{eq:sig_canc_TVlb} \end{align} Here we use \ln(1 - x)\geq -2x, \forall x \in [0,0.796]. This condition is satisfied if and only if 9\varepsilon^2<0.796, \varepsilon <0.29. Thus for \beta =\text{exp}\left[-9\varepsilon^2 T \delta(O_1,\cdots,O_M)\right], we have \text{Pr}_{l \sim p^{(0)}}[L(l) \leq \beta] = 0, which gives the inequality use the fact that 1 - x \leq e^{-x},\forall x \in \mathbb{R}. \begin{align} &1/3\leq 0 +(1 - \beta) = 1 - e^{-9\varepsilon^2 T \delta(O_1,\cdots,O_M)} \leq 9\varepsilon^2 T \delta(O_1,\cdots,O_M) \notag\\ &\Rightarrow T \geq \Omega(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2 \delta(O_1,\cdots,O_M)}), \text{~where~} \delta(O_1,\cdots,O_M):= \sup_{\ket{\phi}} \frac{2}{M}\sum_{i =1}^{M/2}\bra{\phi} O_i \ket{\phi}^2. \label{eq:LB_shadow_eq} \end{align} Now we calculate the value \delta(O_1,\cdots,O_M). Noted that the random variable \bra{\phi} O_i \ket{\phi},\{O_i\}_i \sim \mathcal{O} and \bra{\psi_i} Z_n \ket{\psi_i}, \ket{\psi_i} \sim \text{Haar} has the same distribution. Thus, it is sufficient to discuss the property of function f(\ket{\psi}):= \bra{\psi} Z_n \ket{\psi} with Haar random inputs.

重要Lemma

  Given function f(\ket{\psi}):= \bra{\psi} Z_n \ket{\psi} with independent Haar random inputs, we conclude that \begin{align} &\text{Pr}\left[\left|\frac{1}{R}\sum_{i =1}^{R} f(\ket{\psi_i})^2 - \mathbb{E}_{\ket{\psi} \sim \text{Haar}}\left[ f(\ket{\psi})^2\right]\right| \geq t\right] \leq 2 e^{-R \min(t^2/\lambda^2, t/\lambda)},\\ & \text{where~} \lambda = 288\pi^3/2^n,\quad \mathbb{E}_{\ket{\psi} \sim \text{Haar}} [f(\ket{\psi_i})^2] = \frac{1}{2^n + 1} \end{align}

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. ◻

Now given one state \ket{\phi}, we proved that with high probability \sum_{O \in \mathcal{O}} |\mathcal{O}|^{-1}\bra{\phi} O \ket{\phi}^2 will not deviate from its expectation too much, according to the Lemma [lemma:expon_cent_ineq]. Nevertheless, we hope to prove this property for all states \phi, that is, to bound the deviation of \sup_{\ket{\phi}}\sum_{O \in \mathcal{O}} |\mathcal{O}|^{-1}\bra{\phi} O \ket{\phi}^2. To do this, to first defined an \eta-covering set \mathcal{N}_{\eta} on the n-qubit pure states, as illustrated in Lemma [lemma:covering_on_nqubit].

重要Lemma

  An \eta-covering set \mathcal{N}_{\eta} on the n-qubit pure states is a finite set of n-qubit pure states such that \forall \ket{\phi} \in \mathcal{H}_n, \exists \ket{\psi} \in \mathcal{N}_{\eta}, \\ \text{s.t.~} \|\ket{\phi} - \ket{\psi}\|_2 \leq \eta. The cardinality of \mathcal{N}_{\eta} is upper bounded by |\mathcal{N}_{\eta}| \leq (1 + 2/\eta)^{2^{n+1}}.

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. The set of n-qubit pure states corresponds to the unit sphere in the Hilbert space \mathcal{H}(n) \cong \mathbb{C}^{2^n}. This complex space of dimension 2^n is equivalent to a real space of dimension D = 2 \cdot 2^n = 2^{n+1}. The states are thus points on the unit sphere S^{D-1} in \mathbb{R}^D. Let \mathcal{N}_{\eta} = \{\ket{\psi_1}, \ket{\psi_2}, \dots, \ket{\psi_M}\} be a maximal set of n-qubit pure states such that the Euclidean distance between any two distinct states in the set is greater than \eta. This is known as an \eta-packing. We first argue that this set \mathcal{N}_{\eta} is also an \eta-covering net. If it were not, then \exists \ket{\phi} \in \mathcal{H}_n such that \forall \ket{\psi_i} \in \mathcal{N}_{\eta} ,\|\ket{\phi} - \ket{\psi_i}\|_2 > \eta, which contradicts the assumption that \mathcal{N}_{\eta} is a maximal set. Therefore, any maximal \eta-packing is an \eta-covering net. The problem is now reduced to finding an upper bound on the size M = |\mathcal{N}_{\eta}| of such a packing. Consider a set of open balls \{B(\ket{\psi_i}, \eta/2)\}_{i=1}^M of radius \eta/2 centered at each point of our set \mathcal{N}_{\eta}. Since for any i \neq j, we have \|\ket{\psi_i} - \ket{\psi_j}\|_2 > \eta, the triangle inequality implies that these balls are disjoint. All these disjoint balls are contained within a larger ball of radius 1 + \eta/2 centered at the origin. This is because each \ket{\psi_i} is on the unit sphere (norm 1), and any point in the ball B(\ket{\psi_i}, \eta/2) has a norm of at most \|\ket{\psi_i}\|_2 + \eta/2 = 1 + \eta/2. The total volume of these M disjoint balls cannot exceed the volume of the larger containing ball. Let V_D(r) be the volume of a D-dimensional ball of radius r. We have \sum_{i=1}^M V_D(\eta/2) \le V_D(1 + \eta/2). Since all the small balls have the same volume, this simplifies to M \cdot V_D(\eta/2) \le V_D(1 + \eta/2). The volume of a D-dimensional ball of radius r is given by C_D r^D for some constant C_D that depends only on the dimension D. Thus, we can write M \cdot C_D (\eta/2)^D \le C_D (1 + \eta/2)^D. Canceling the constant C_D and substituting back the dimension D = 2^{n+1}, we get the upper bound on M \begin{align} |\mathcal{N}_{\eta}| = M \le \frac{(1 + \eta/2)^D}{(\eta/2)^D} = \left(\frac{1 + \eta/2}{\eta/2}\right)^D = \left(1 + \frac{2}{\eta}\right)^D. \end{align} ◻

Then the low-deviation condition that satisfied for arbitrary \ket{\phi} \in \mathcal{H}(n) also satisfied on set \mathcal{N}_{\eta}, only with a |\mathcal{N}_\eta| larger error probability. After this, we show that the function g(\ket{\phi}):=\sum_{O \in \mathcal{O}} |\mathcal{O}|^{-1}\bra{\phi} O \ket{\phi}^2 is Lipschitz continuous, which means that the difference of function value is upper bounded by the variables difference. Combining the Lipschitz continuity and the property of the \eta-covering, we show upper bounds for the value \sup_{\ket{\phi}}\sum_{O \in \mathcal{O}} |\mathcal{O}|^{-1}\bra{\phi} O \ket{\phi}^2, as rigrously illustrated in Lemma [lemma:point_to_uniform].

重要Lemma

  Given an L-Lipschitz continuous function f:V \to \mathbb{R} on metric space V and an \eta-covering set \mathcal{N}_{\eta} of V, if \forall x \in \mathcal{N}_{\eta}, |f(x) - c| < t, then \forall x \in V, |f(x) - c| < t + L \eta.

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. By definition, we know that \forall x \in V, \exists r_x \in \mathcal{N}_{\eta} \text{~s.t.~} |r_x - x| \leq \eta. Then we conclude \begin{align} \forall x \in V, |f(x) - c| &\leq |f(x) - f(r_x)| + |f(r_x) - c|\leq L\|x - r_x\| + t \leq L\eta + t. \end{align} ◻

If we further

重要Theorem

Given a uniform distribution on M Pauli observables \mathcal{A}:=\{P_1,\cdots,P_M\}, any single-copy learning algorithm that predict \{\text{tr}(\rho P)\}_{P \sim \mathcal{A}} with \varepsilon-additive error and 2/3 success probability must use T \geq \Omega \left(\varepsilon^{-2} \min\{M/\log M, 2^n\}\right) samples.

1.4.3 Pauli mixed states

Given a subset \mathcal{O} \subset \mathcal{P}(n), try to discriminate (i). A set of state {S}_{\mathcal{O}}:=\{\sigma_{P}:=(\mathbb{I}+ 3\varepsilon P)/d\}_{P \in \mathcal{O}} and (ii) \rho = \mathbb{I}/2^n with confidence 1 - \delta.

1.4.4 Single replica.

Similarly, we set up hard distributions as uniform distribution on signed Pauli operators \{+1,-1\}\times \mathcal{O}, where \mathcal{O} \subset \{\mathbb{I},X,Y,Z\}. Follow the same procedure of Eq.[eq:sig_canc_TVlb], we then calculate its rank-1 POVM leaves likelihood as: \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{s,P} L_{s,P}(l) \geq \exp\left[-18\varepsilon^2T \sup_{\ket{\phi}} \mathbb{E}_{P\in \mathrm{Uniform}(\mathcal{O})} \bra{\phi} P \ket{\phi}^2\right]. \end{align} In the case of \mathcal{O} = \mathcal{P}_n, we use the identity \mathbb{E}_{P\in \mathrm{Uniform}(\mathcal{P}_n)} \bra{\phi} P \ket{\phi}^2 \\ =\bra{\phi}\bra{\phi} 4^{-n}\sum_{P\in \mathcal{P}_n}P \otimes P\ket{\phi}\ket{\phi} and \sum_{P\in \mathcal{P}_n}P \otimes P = 2^{n}\mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}. We conclude that \mathbb{E}_{s,P} L_{s,P}(l) \geq e^{-18\varepsilon^2 T 2^{-n}},\forall l. Use Lemma [lemma:UB_TVD], we conclude that for all choice of single-copy POVM, \|p_{\mathbb{I}/d} - \mathbb{E}_{s,P}p_{\rho_{s,P}}\|_{\mathrm{tvd}} \leq 1 - e^{-18\varepsilon^2 T 2^{-n}}. This means that to reach confidence 1/2 + \delta/2, we have to set 1 - e^{-18\varepsilon^2 T 2^{-n}} \geq \delta \Rightarrow T \geq 18^{-1}\times 2^n \varepsilon^{-2}\ln(1 - \delta).

According to Theorem [theo:mart_distinguish_lb], we can also calculate its \chi-squared divergence given ensemble \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O} on the subset of Pauli operators \mathcal{O}: \begin{align} \delta_{\mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} &:= \max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}}\mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} \mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\sigma_P F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} - 1\right]^2= \max_{F_s \succ 0 }\sum_{s} \frac{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})}{d}\mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\frac{\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon P}{d}F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})/d} - 1\right]^2 \notag\\ &= 9\varepsilon^2 \max_{F_s \succ 0 }\sum_{s} \frac{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})}{d}\mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}({P}F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})}\right]^2 = {9\varepsilon^2} \max_{F_s \succ 0 }\mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} \sum_{s} \frac{\left[\mathrm{tr}({P}F_{s})\right]^2}{{d}\cdot \mathrm{tr}(F_{s})}. \end{align} Since F_s includes all the rank-1 POVMs and each POVMs with rank greater than 1 can be equivalently realized using rank-1 POVMs with undecreasing discrimination efficiency, as shown in Lemma [lemma:POVM_r1_reduction]. We can plug in F_s = 2^{n}w_s \ket{\psi_s}\!\bra{\psi_s} with \{w_s\} a valid distribution and conclude the same result: \begin{align} \max_{F_s \succ 0 }\mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} \sum_{s} \frac{\left[\mathrm{tr}({P}F_{s})\right]^2}{{d}\cdot \mathrm{tr}(F_{s})} &= \max_{\ket{\psi_s}}\mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} \sum_{s}w_s{\left[\bra{\psi_s}{P}\ket{\psi_s}\right]^2} = \max_{\ket{\phi}}\mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} {\bra{\phi}{P}\ket{\phi}^2} \\ &\sim \Omega(2^{-n}) \text{~if~} \mathcal{O} = \mathcal{P}_n, \mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{O}} = \mathrm{Uniform}(\mathcal{O}). \end{align} Then based on Lemma [theo:mart_distinguish_lb], T\geq 2^n. Note that such a martingale analysis do not directly applied to purity-identity test, which has a constant \chi-squared divergence, as calculated below: \begin{align} \delta_{\mathrm{Haar}} &= \max_{F_s \succ 0 }\sum_{s} \frac{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})}{d}\mathbb{E}_{\ket{\psi}\sim \mathrm{Haar}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\ket{\psi}\!\bra{\psi}F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})/d} - 1\right]^2=\max_{F_s \succ 0 }\sum_{s} \mathbb{E}_{\ket{\psi}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\ket{\psi}\!\bra{\psi}^{\otimes 2}F_{s}\otimes F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})/d}\right]- 1\\ &=\max_{\ket{\psi_s} }\sum_{s} d^2w_s\mathbb{E}_{\ket{\psi}} \left[{\mathrm{tr}({\psi}^{\otimes 2} \psi_s^{\otimes 2})}\right]- 1 = \frac{2d^2}{d(d+1)} - 1 = \frac{d-1}{d+1} \sim \Omega(1). \end{align} This great difference between ensemble supports on \{(\mathbb{I}+ 3\varepsilon O)/2^n\}_{O \in \mathcal{O}} and Haar random state supports on \{\psi\} is because the probability of the latter one is more concentrated. \begin{align*} p_{\mathrm{Haar}}(\psi_s) =\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\ket{\psi}\!\bra{\psi}\psi_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbb{I}/d\cdot \psi_{s})}= d |\langle {\psi}|{\psi_s}\rangle|^2 \in[0,d], \, p_{\mathcal{P}}(\psi_s) =\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\frac{\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon P}{d}\psi_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbb{I}/d\psi_{s})}=1 + 3\varepsilon\langle{\psi_s}|P|{\psi_s}\rangle \in [1- 3\varepsilon, 1+ 3\varepsilon]. \end{align*}

1.5 Haar-assembled ensembles and its distinguishablity

1.5.1 Properties of Haar-assembled ensembles

The lower bound of many problem are find by first reduce this problem to distinguishing one specific state with a state ensemble. One useful state ensembles are constructed from reducing Haar random state.

注记Definition

Given a D = 2^{n + \log(1/\varepsilon)} = d\cdot \varepsilon^{-1} dimensional Haar random state \ket{H} \sim \mathrm{Haar}(D). The 2^n-dimensional reduced Haar-induced (RH) state is defined as \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}:=\{\text{tr}_{>n} \ket{H}\!\bra{H}\}_{\ket{H} \sim \mathrm{Haar}(D)}.

Depending on the scale of reduced parts, the RH-ensemble has tunable purity. We then show in Lemma [lemma:purity_of_RH] that the random variable \mathrm{tr}(\rho^2), \rho \sim \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{RH}}_{\varepsilon} is well concentrated and separate from maximum mixed state purity 1/d. This statement is useful to proving the reduction of \mathrm{tr}(\rho^2) problem.

重要Lemma

The c-copy average of \rho \in \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon} writes: \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}} \rho^{\otimes c} = \frac{1}{D^{\uparrow c}}\sum_{\pi \in S_c} \varepsilon^{-c(\pi)}\mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{d}. \end{align} Furthermore, its purity average and variance writes: \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}} \mathrm{tr}(\rho^2) = \frac{2^n\varepsilon + 1}{2^n + \varepsilon},\quad \mathrm{Var}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}} [\mathrm{tr}(\rho^2)] = \frac{2(2^{2n} - 1)(1/\varepsilon^2-1)}{(2^n/\varepsilon + 1)^2 (2^n/\varepsilon+2)(2^n/\varepsilon+3)}. \end{align}

证明. Proof. On going proof... \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}}\rho^{\otimes c}&=\mathbb{E}_{H \sim \mathrm{Haar}(D)}(\text{tr}_{>n} \ket{H}\!\bra{H})^{\otimes c} = \frac{1}{D^{\uparrow c}}\mathrm{tr}_{>n}(\sum_{\pi \in S_c} \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{d} \otimes \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{\varepsilon^{-1}})=\frac{1}{D^{\uparrow c}}\sum_{\pi \in S_c} \varepsilon^{-c(\pi)}\mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{d}. \end{align} Then the average of purity can be directly calculate as \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}} \mathrm{tr}(\rho^2) &=\mathrm{tr}\left(\frac{\varepsilon^{-2} \mathbb{I}_{n}^{\otimes 2}+\varepsilon^{-1} \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}}{D(D+1)} \cdot \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}\right) = \frac{\varepsilon^{-2} 2^n + \varepsilon^{-1} 2^{2n}}{2^n\varepsilon^{-1}(2^n \varepsilon^{-1}+1)}= \frac{2^n\varepsilon + 1}{2^n + \varepsilon},\\ \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}} [\mathrm{tr}(\rho^2)]^2&=\mathrm{tr}\left(\frac{ \sum_{\pi \in S_4}{\varepsilon^{-c(\pi)}\mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{d}}}{D(D+1)(D+2)(D+3)}\mathbb{P}_{(12)(34)}^{d}\right)=\frac{\sum_{\pi \in S_4}d^{c(\pi \cdot (12)(34))}(1/\varepsilon)^{c(\pi)}}{D(D+1)(D+2)(D+3)}. \end{align} Here c(\pi) count the number of cycles for permutation \pi. State ensembles can also be constructed from mixing independent Haar random state.

注记Definition

Given a probability \{p_r\}_{r = 0}^{m}, defined the multi-variant Haar ensemble (MH) as the mix states \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{p}}:=\{p_0 {\mathbb{I}(d)}/{d} + \sum_{j = 1}^{m} p_j \psi_j\}_{\psi_j \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d)}.

As a generalization of Lemma [lemma:purity_of_RH], we then try to conclude that for an arbitrary k-replica operator O, it is possible to construct two MH-ensemble \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{p}},\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{q}} such that \{\mathrm{tr}(O\rho^k)\}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{p}}} and \{\mathrm{tr}(O\rho^k)\}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{q}}} are well separated and both well concentrated. To prove this, we rewrite the k-replica of MH-ensembles as \begin{align} \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH},\otimes k}_{m} = \left\{\sum_{A_0 \cup \cdots \cup A_m = \{1,\cdots,k\}}\left(p_0^{|A_0|}\prod_{r = 1}^{m} p_r^{ |A_r|}\right)\cdot \psi^{\otimes A_1}_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes \psi^{\otimes A_m}_m \otimes \left(\frac{\mathbb{I}(d)}{d}\right)^{\otimes A_0}\right\}_{\psi_r \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d)},\label{eq:k_rep_MH} \end{align} where A_0 \cup \cdots \cup A_m = \{1,\cdots,k\} go over all (m+1)-partition of k elements and \psi_r^{A_r} means distributing state \psi_r at elements within A_r. If we use j = (A_1,\cdots,A_m,A_0) to denote a partition of \{1,\cdots,k\} and p_j = p_0^{|A_0|}\prod_{r = 1}^{m} p_r^{ |A_r|} to denote the mixing rate, and use unitary U_j to sort the qudits in an order such that \psi_1,\psi_2,\cdots,\psi_m supports on \{1,\cdots,|A_1|\},\{|A_1|+1,\cdots,|A_1|+|A_2|\}, \cdots,\{|A_{m}|+1,\cdots,k\} respectively, we get the extended Haar-induced ensemble below.

注记Definition

Given m Haar random state \{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_m\}, each with dimension d_1,\cdots,d_m, multiplicity parameter \mathbf{a} \in (\mathbb{Z}_+)^{m} =(a_1,\cdots,a_m), and the r-dimensional complement state \tau such that \sum_{k=1}^m a_k\cdot d_k + r = D. A D-dimensional (\mathbf{a}^{(j)}, \tau^{(j)}) extended Haar-induced (EH) ensemble is an ensemble of D-dimensional mixed state that is specified by a \mathcal{U} := \{p_j,U_j\}_{j = 1}^J unitary mixing of D-dimensional pure state \psi_1^{\otimes a_1} \otimes \cdots\otimes \psi_m^{\otimes a_m} \otimes \tau, written as \begin{align} \mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{U},\mathbf{a}, \tau} := \{\sum_{j= 1}^J p_j U_j \psi_1^{\otimes a^{(j)}_1} \otimes \cdots\otimes \psi_m^{\otimes a^{(j)}_m} \otimes \tau^{(j)} U_j^\dagger\}_{\psi_k \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d_k)}. \end{align}

Thus, it is sufficient to prove that \mathrm{tr}(O\sigma), \sigma \sim \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{EH}}_{\mathbf{a}} is separated and concentrated. For the separated part, we prove the lemma below

重要Lemma

Suppose \forall i= 1,\cdots,k, \sum_{r = 1}^m p_r^{i} = \sum_{r = 1}^m q_r^{i} and p_0 = q_0, the multi-variant Haar induced ensemble \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{p}} and \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{q}} satisfied \begin{align} &\forall i= 1,\cdots,k, \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{p}}} \rho^i - \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{q}}} \rho^i = 0\\ &\mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{p}}} \rho^{k+1} - \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{q}}} \rho^{k+1} = (\sum_{r=1}^m p_r^{k+1} - \sum_{r=1}^m q_r^{k+1}) \Delta_{k+1}\\ \end{align}

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. Refer to Eq. [eq:k_rep_MH], we conclude that ◻

Then we show the lemma below for the bound of specific O

重要Lemma

Given k+1 qudit operator O, then \begin{align} \left|\sum_{\pi \in S_{k+1}^{\mathrm{circ}}} c_{\pi} (O) - \mathrm{tr}(O \Delta_{k+1})\right| \leq \frac{(k+1)^{2k}}{d}. \end{align}

1.5.2 Pure-Identity test

Perhaps the most simple one are the maximum mixed state \mathbb{I}(d)/d with all possible pure state \ket{\psi}.

Design an algorithm using restrained measurements that, given access to a device guaranteed to prepare a state that is either (i)one of pure states \ket{\psi} or (ii) the maximally mixed state d^{-1}\mathbb{I}, can distinguish between these two cases with an error of at most 1/2-\varepsilon.

Based on Lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound], in the following we relax the problem with a problem ensemble \ket{\psi} \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d). This reduction is sufficient, while not fully characterize the hardness of pure-identity test. To fully pinned down the hardness, ones should build arbitrary ensemble on pure states and check the hardness. Thus,

1.5.3 The 1-replica strategy.

We first consider the 1-replica restriction on measurements.

For a T-round 1-replica adaptive strategy M_s = F^{u_1}_{s_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes F^{u_T}_{s_T}, we use Lemma [lemma:UB_TVD] and lower bounds its leaves’ likelihood: \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\psi} L_{\psi} = \mathbb{E}_{{\psi} \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d)}\frac{d^{T}\mathrm{tr}(M_s \ket{\psi}\!\bra{\psi}^{\otimes T})}{\mathrm{tr}(M_s)} = \frac{d^T}{d(d+1)\cdots(d+T-1)} \frac{\mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_T}\mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} \cdot M_s\right)}{\mathrm{tr}\left( \bigotimes_{t = 1}^T\left[\mathbb{I}(d)\right]\cdot M_s\right)}.\label{eq:midres_1repPItest} \end{align} To do this, we upper bounds each term in the RHS of Eq.[eq:midres_1repPItest]. For the constant, we conclude that \begin{align} \frac{d^T}{d(d+1)\cdots(d+T-1)}&=\left(1 \cdot (1+\frac{1}{d})\cdots(1+\frac{T-1}{d})\right)^{-1}\geq (1 + T/d)^{-T} \notag \\ &=e^{-T\ln(1 + T/d)} \geq e^{-T^2/d}. \label{eq:lb_upfrac} \end{align} For the second term, we decomposed M_s into its eigenvector through defining F_{s_j}^{u_j} =\sum_{s}\lambda_{j,s}{v_{j,s}} with \lambda_{j,s_j}\geq 0 and writes \begin{align} {\mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_T}\mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} \cdot M_s\right)} &= T!\cdot\sum_{s_1,\cdots,s_T}\lambda_{1,s_1}\cdots\lambda_{T,s_T} \mathrm{tr}\left(\Pi_{sym}{v_{1,s_1} \otimes\cdots\otimes v_{T,s_T}}\right)\\ &\geq \sum_{s_1,\cdots,s_T}\lambda_{1,s_1}\cdots \lambda_{T,s_T}={\mathrm{tr}\left( \bigotimes_{t = 1}^T\left[\mathbb{I}(d)\right]\cdot M_s\right)} \end{align} Here in the second line we show the lemma below:

重要Lemma

For T numbers of d-qudit pure states \ket{\psi_1}, \cdots,\ket{\psi_T} and the symmetrization projector \Pi_{\mathrm{sym},T} := (T!)^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in S_T} \mathbb{P}^{d}_{\pi}, we conclude that \text{tr}\left(\Pi_{\mathrm{sym},T}\bigotimes_{t = 1}^T \ket{\psi_t} \!\bra{\psi_t}\right) \geq (T!)^{-1}.

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. ◻

Thus, we conclude that max_{\{M_s = \otimes_{t=1}^{T}F_{s_t}^{u_t}\}_s}\|p_{\mathbb{I}} - p_{\psi}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \leq 1 - \min_{\{M_s\}_s, s} \mathbb{E}_{\psi} L_{\psi}(s) \leq 1 - e^{-T^2/d} \leq T^2/d based on the first equation in Lemma [lemma:UB_TVD]. This means that to reach success rate 1/2 + \varepsilon, T^2/d \geq 2\varepsilon must be satisfied, thus gives T \geq \mathcal{O}({\sqrt{d}}).

1.5.4 The 2-replica strategy with k-memory.

Now we consider a fine-tuned setting of the measurement restriction. We consider d = 2^n as n-qubits and allow 2-replica measurements but restrained on the \{M_s\}_s \subset \mathcal{M}_{2,n}^k as defined in definition [def:crep_kmem_POVMs]. Similar to the 1-replica analysis, we first write its Haar-average leaf likelihood \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\psi} L_{\psi} &= \mathbb{E}_{{\psi} \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d)}\frac{d^{2T}\mathrm{tr}(M_s \ket{\psi}\!\bra{\psi}^{\otimes 2T})}{\mathrm{tr}(M_s)} = \frac{d^{2T}}{d(d+1)\cdots(d+2T-1)} \frac{\mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_{2T}}\mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} \cdot M_s\right)}{\mathrm{tr}\left( \bigotimes_{t = 1}^T\left[\mathbb{I}(d)\right]\cdot M_s\right)}\\ &\geq e^{-4d^{-1}T^2}\cdot \frac{\mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_{2T}}\mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} \cdot M_s\right)}{\mathrm{tr}\left( S_2^{\otimes T}\cdot M_s\right)} \cdot\prod_{t = 1}^T \frac{\mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_2}\mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} \cdot F_{s_t}^{u_t}\right)}{\mathrm{tr}\left(F_{s_t}^{u_t}\right)}\\ &\geq (1{-4d^{-1}T^2})\cdot \prod_{t = 1}^T \frac{\mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_2}\mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} \cdot F_{s_t}^{u_t}\right)}{\mathrm{tr}\left(F_{s_t}^{u_t}\right)}\geq (1{-4d^{-1}T^2})\left(\frac{2^{2n}}{2^n(2^n+1)}\right)^T \prod_{t = 1}^T \frac{\mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_2}\mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} \cdot F_{s_t}^{u_t}\right)}{\mathrm{tr}\left(F_{s_t}^{u_t}\right)} \label{eq:2rep_kmemo_leaflike} \end{align} Here in the second line we do the same calculation of Eq.[eq:lb_upfrac] and insert a value \mathrm{tr}\left( S_2^{\otimes T}\cdot M_s\right) in the denominator. The third line is bounded by Lemma [lemma:sepa_S_smaller] below, as a generalization of Lemma [lemma:sym_prod_lb].

重要Lemma

Given a semi-positive operator F = F_A \otimes F_B that separable on set of qudits A and qudits B. Denote S_a = \sum_{\pi \in S_{|A|}} \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{d} and similar for S_B,S_{A+B}. Then \mathrm{tr}\left({S_A \otimes S_B F}\right) \leq \mathrm{tr}\left({S_{A+B}F}\right).

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. ◻

For the second inequality in Eq. [eq:2rep_kmemo_leaflike], we noted that if we use M_s = \otimes_{t = 1}^T F_{s_t}^{u_t} to discriminate \rho = \mathbb{I}(d^2)/d^2 and \sigma = [2^n(2^n+1)]^{-1}(\mathbb{I}_n^{\otimes 2} + \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}) in the 2-replica space \mathcal{H}(d^2), the likelihood function satisfied: \begin{align} L'(s) =\left(\frac{2^{2n}}{2^n(2^n+1)}\right)^T \prod_{t = 1}^T \frac{\mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_2}\mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} \cdot F_{s_t}^{u_t}\right)}{\mathrm{tr}\left(F_{s_t}^{u_t}\right)}. \end{align} It is thus sufficient to show a upper bound for L'. Refer to Lemma [lemma:UB_Ltail], we consider the chi-squared divergence with \rho and \sigma. \begin{align} \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\sigma}&=\max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}^{k}_{2,n}}\sum_{s}\frac{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})}{4^n}\left[\frac{2^{n}\mathrm{tr}\left[(\mathbb{I}_n^{\otimes 2} + \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n})F_{s}\right]}{(2^n+1)\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})} - 1\right]^2 \notag\\ &=\max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}^{k}_{2,n}}\sum_{s} \frac{\mathrm{tr}(F_s)}{4^n}(2^n+1)^{-2}\left[2^n \frac{\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n} F_s)}{\mathrm{tr}(F_s)} - 1\right]^2\notag\\ &=\max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}^{k}_{2,n}}\frac{1}{4^n}(2^n+1)^{-2}\left[4^n \sum_{s} \frac{[\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n} F_s)]^2}{\mathrm{tr}(F_s)} - 2 \times 2^n {\mathrm{tr}\left(\mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}\sum_{s}F_s\right)} + \mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{s}F_s\right)\right]\notag\\ &=\frac{1}{(2^n+1)^{2}}\left[\max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}^{k}_{2,n}} \sum_{s} \frac{[\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n} F_s)]^2}{\mathrm{tr}(F_s)} - 1\right]. \end{align} Here in the last line, we use \sum_{s} F_s = \mathbb{I}_{2n} and \text{tr}(\mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}) = 2^n. If Bell measurements F_{\mathbf{s}} = \Phi_{\mathbf{s}} is allowed, we can verify that \sum_{\mathbf{s}}[\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n} \Phi_{\mathbf{s}})]^2/{\mathrm{tr}(\Phi_{\mathbf{s}})} = 4^n. However, the k-memeory restriction on F_s prevent this measurement and imposed a upper bound on the MPS-rank of projected basis, as depicted in Lemma [lemma:lowMPS_SWAPproduct]. This lower bounds the maximum value as \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\sigma} \leq 2^{k-n} - 2^{-2n}. Based on Lemma [lemma:UB_Ltail], we conclude that \mathrm{Pr}_{l \sim p_{\mathbb{I}, \mathcal{T}}}(L'(l) \geq 1 - c_1) \geq 1 - c_2 - c_3\cdot (2^{k-n} - 2^{-2n})T. Then plug into Eq.[eq:2rep_kmemo_leaflike] to replace L' by \mathbb{\psi}L_{\psi}, we conclude that \forall c_1\in (0,1/3), c_2 > 0, \exists c_3>0 such that \mathrm{Pr}_{l \sim p_{\mathbb{I}, \mathcal{T}}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\psi} L_{\psi}(l) \leq (1{-4d^{-1}T^2})(1 - c_1)\right] \leq c_2 + c_3\cdot (2^{k-n} - 2^{-2n})T. Finally, using the second identity in Lemma [lemma:UB_TVD] for a being a unique element with p^{(a)} = \mathbb{E}_{\psi} p_{\psi, \mathcal{T}}, we must have \begin{align} 2\varepsilon \leq \|p_{\mathbb{I}, \mathcal{T}} - \mathbb{E}_{\psi} p_{\psi, \mathcal{T}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} &\leq c_2 + c_3\cdot (2^{k-n} - 2^{-2n})T + 1 - (1{-4\times 2^{-n}T^2})(1 - c_1) \end{align} Without lose of generality, we set \varepsilon = 1/6, i.e., to be 1/6 better than random guessing. We have 0.2 + 2\gamma T ( -2^{-2n} + 2^{k - n})+3.6\times 2^{-n} T^2 > 1/3, where we take c_1= c_2 = 0.1,c_3 = \gamma>0. This gives the inequality \begin{align} \label{eq:T_ineq} T^2 + \frac{\gamma(-2^{-n} + 2^k)}{1.8} T - \frac{2^n}{54} >0. \end{align} We conclude that there exist constants a_1,a_2 that satisfy 0<a_1 < a_2 \leq (1/2)\cdot [\sqrt{(\gamma /1.8)^2 + 1/9} - \gamma/1.8], such that T > \min\{a_12^{n/2}, a_22^{n-k}\} must be satisfied otherwise \begin{align} LHS \leq a_1^2 2^n + \frac{\gamma }{1.8}(a_2 2^n) - \frac{2^n}{54}\leq (a_1^2 + \gamma \frac{a_2}{1.8}-1/54)2^n<(a_2^2 + \frac{\gamma}{1.8}a_2-1/54)2^n < 0, \end{align} which is contradictory with Eq. [eq:T_ineq]. This proves the lower bound T \geq \Omega(\min\{2^{n/2}, 2^{n-k}\}) for the 2-copy k-memory adaptive strategy that solve the purity-identity test problem with 2/3 correct rate.

1.5.5 MH-ensemble test.

Now we consider a general case where we supposed to distinguish an arbitrary element within MH ensemble from its average.

Design an algorithm that distinguishes between two cases below using restrained measurements at error rate less than 1/2-\varepsilon. (i)One of state within \mathcal{E}_{p} := \{p_0 {\mathbb{I}(d)}/{d} + \sum_{j = 1}^{m} p_j \psi_j\} or (ii) One of state within \mathcal{E}_{q}:=\{q_0 {\mathbb{I}(d)}/{d} + \sum_{j = 1}^{m} q_j \psi_j\}

It is easy to check that pure-identity test in Problem [prob:2k_PItest] is a special case of Problem [prob:MHtest], with p_1 = 1, p_m = 0,\forall m \neq 1 and q_0 = 1, q_m = 0,\forall m \neq 0. However, this problem might be too hard, as \mathcal{E}_{p} \cap \mathcal{E}_{q}\neq \emptyset if there exist a distribution \lambda such that \lambda \succ \{p_j/(1 - p_0)\}_j and \lambda \succ \{q_j/(1-q_0)\}_j. We thus relax this problem by setting the problem ensemble as \psi_{j} \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d), \forall j=1,\cdots,m. To further fix this testing problem, we also imposed the rank-k condition: \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\psi_j\sim \mathrm{Haar}(d)} \left(p_0 {\mathbb{I}(d)}/{d} + \sum_{j = 1}^{m} p_j \psi_j\right)^{\otimes k} = \mathbb{E}_{\psi_j\sim \mathrm{Haar}(d)} \left(q_0 {\mathbb{I}(d)}/{d} + \sum_{j = 1}^{m} q_j \psi_j\right)^{\otimes k} \end{align}

1.5.6 The k-replica strategy.

We directly discuss its lower bound under the k-replica measurement restrictions.

1.5.7 EH-ensemble test.

Design an algorithm using restrained measurements to distinguish between two cases below with an error no more than 1/2-\varepsilon.(i)one of the states \rho \in \mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{U},\mathbf{a},\tau} or (ii) the average mixed state \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{U},\mathbf{a},\tau} }\rho.

Suppose we adapt the adaptive strategy \mathcal{T} with corresponding measurement M_s = F^{u_1}_{s_1}\otimes \cdots \otimes F^{u_T}_{s_T}, the measurement results give two distribution: \begin{align} p_0(s) = \mathrm{tr}\left[ M_s \sum_{\mathbf{j} \in [J]^T}\left(\prod_{t = 1}^T p_{j_t}\right) \bigotimes_{t=1}^{T} \mathbb{E}{\sigma_{j_t}}\right],\quad p_{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_m}(s) = \mathrm{tr}\left[ M_s \sum_{\mathbf{j} \in [J]^T}\left(\prod_{t = 1}^T p_{j_t}\right) \bigotimes_{t=1}^{T} {\sigma_{j_t}}\right], \end{align} where we use abbreviation \sigma_{j_t} = U_{j_t} \psi_{1}^{\otimes a_{1}^{(j_t)}} \otimes \cdots \otimes \psi_{m}^{\otimes a_{m}^{(j_t)}} \otimes \tau^{(j_t)} U_{j_t}^\dagger and \mathbb{E}\sigma_{j_t} = \mathbb{E}_{\psi_j \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d_j)} U_{j_t} \psi_{1}^{\otimes a_{1}^{(j_t)}} \otimes \cdots \otimes \psi_{m}^{\otimes a_{m}^{(j_t)}} \otimes \tau^{(j_t)} U_{j_t}^\dagger. Lower bounding the problem [prob:EAtest] require the analysis of the similarity between the distribution p_{0} and \{p_{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_m}\}_{\psi_j}. Based on Lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound], we choose \psi_k \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d_k). Then we remove the effects of mixing probability p_j in the EH-ensemble through the inequality \begin{align} \|p_{0} - \mathbb{E}p_{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_m}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \leq \sum_{j_1,\cdots,j_T \in [J]}\left(\prod_{t = 1}^T p_{j_t}\right) \|q_{0,\mathbf{j}} - \mathbb{E}q_{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_m,\mathbf{j}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{align} It is sufficient to find an upper bound of \|q_{0,\mathbf{j}} - \mathbb{E} q_{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_m,\mathbf{j}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} for an arbitrary fixed choice of \mathbf{j}. The probability q_{0,\mathbf{j}} = \mathrm{tr}\left[ M_s \bigotimes_{t=1}^{T} \mathbb{E}{\sigma_{j_t}}\right] and q_{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_m,\mathbf{j}} = \mathrm{tr}\left[ M_s \bigotimes_{t=1}^{T} {\sigma_{j_t}}\right] are the measurement results distribution with testing strategy \{M_s\}_s for two different input states. Defining V = U_{j_1}\otimes \cdots \otimes U_{j_T}, an m \times T matrix \mathbf{A} with A_{k,t} := a_{k}^{(j_t)}, {A}_{r,:} = a_{r}^{(j_1)} +\cdots+ a_{r}^{(j_T)}, and \zeta = \bigotimes_{t = 1}^T \tau^{(j_t)}, this reduces the EH-ensemble to a two-state discrimination problem.

Design an algorithm using restrained single-replica measurements that can distinguish between these two states below with an error of at most 1/2-\varepsilon: (i) \rho_{\mathbf{j}} =V \left[\mathbb{E} \psi_1^{\otimes A_{1,:}} \otimes \cdots\otimes \psi_m^{\otimes A_{m,:}} \otimes \xi \right] V^\dagger or (ii) \sigma_{\mathbf{j}} = V \left[\bigotimes_{t = 1}^T \left(\mathbb{E} \psi_{1}^{\otimes A_{1,t}} \otimes \cdots \otimes \psi_{m}^{\otimes A_{m,t}} \right) \otimes \xi \right] V^\dagger.

by the virtue of the first inequality in Lemma [lemma:UB_TVD] and it is sufficient to show an upper bound for their likelihood \begin{align} \|q_{0,\mathbf{j}} - \mathbb{E} q_{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_m,\mathbf{j}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} &\leq 1- \min_{s}\frac{\mathrm{tr}(M_s \rho_{\mathbf{j}})}{\mathrm{tr}(M_s \sigma_{\mathbf{j}})} = 1 - \min_{s}\frac{\mathrm{tr}(M'_s \mathbb{E} \psi_1^{\otimes A_{1,:}} \otimes \cdots\otimes \psi_m^{\otimes A_{m,:}} )}{\mathrm{tr}(M'_s \bigotimes_{t = 1}^T \left[\mathbb{E} \psi_{1}^{\otimes A_{1,t}} \otimes \cdots \otimes \psi_{m}^{\otimes A_{m,t}} \right])}\\ &=1 - \frac{\prod_{t = 1}^T \left[d_1^{\uparrow A_{1,t}}\cdots d_m^{\uparrow A_{m,t}}\right]}{d_1^{\uparrow A_{1,:}}\cdots d_m^{\uparrow A_{m,:}}}\max_{s}\frac{\mathrm{tr}(M'_s S^{A_{1,:}} \otimes \cdots\otimes S^{A_{m,:}} )}{\mathrm{tr}(M'_s \bigotimes_{t = 1}^T \left[ S^{A_{1,t}} \otimes \cdots \otimes S^{A_{m,t}} \right])},\label{eq:midres_EHI} \end{align} where we use S^{A} to denote the centralizer of permutations S_{A} = \sum_{\pi \in S_{A}} \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{d} that supports on the qudits counted by A. We then show the lower bound of the LHS in Eq. [eq:midres_EHI] through two lemmas below.

重要Lemma

Given A = \cup_{k = 1}^{m} \cup_{t = 1}^T A_{k,t} as a partition of qudits set A. Ensure that the qudits in subset \cup_{t} A_{k,t} have the same dimension d_k, such that both A_{k,t} and \cup_{t} A_{k,t} forms the identical qudits set. Denotes S^{A_{k,t}},S^{A_{k,:}} as the representation of permutation group S_{|A_{k,t}|}, S_{A_{k,:}} on these identical qudits sets. Then for arbitrary operator M that is the product form under the separation \left(\cup_{k = 1}^{m}A_{k,1}\right) \cup \cdots \cup \left(\cup_{k = 1}^{m}A_{k,T}\right), we have: \begin{align} {\mathrm{tr}(M S^{A_{1,:}} \otimes \cdots\otimes S^{A_{m,:}} )} \leq {\mathrm{tr}(M \bigotimes_{t = 1}^T \left[ S^{A_{1,t}} \otimes \cdots \otimes S^{A_{m,t}} \right])}. \end{align}
