重要Lemma

Given a length-T vector (v_1,\cdots,v_T) with v_i \in \mathbb{Z}_+, the inequality below is satisfied: \begin{align} \frac{d^{\uparrow y_1} \cdots d^{\uparrow y_T}}{ d^{\uparrow y_1 + \cdots + y_T} } \geq e^{-d^{-1} \left(\sum_{t = 1}^T y_t\right)^2}. \end{align}

1.5.8 RH-ensemble test

Design an algorithm using restrained measurements to distinguish between two cases below with success rate 1/2+\delta.(i)the maximum mixed state \mathbb{I}/d or (ii) states set with problem ensemble \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}.

1.5.9 Subspace RH-ensemble test

Given RH ensemble \mathcal{E}_{1 - R\delta}, \mathcal{E}_{L\delta}, as defined in Problem [prob:RHtest], with R = (2^{n-1} + 1)/(2^{n-1} - 1 +\delta) and L = (1 - 4^{-n+1} - 2^{-n+1} \delta)^{-1}, try to design an algorithm that \forall C \in \mathcal{C}, discriminates two subspace-RH ensembles below: \begin{align} &\mathcal{E}_{(1,0),C} := \left\{\sigma_{(1,0),C}:= C \left[\frac{1}{2} \ket{0}\!\bra{0} \otimes \psi + \frac{1}{2} \ket{1}\!\bra{1} \otimes (\mathbb{I}/2^{n-1}) \right] C^{\dagger}\right\}_{\psi \sim \mathrm{Haar}_{n-1}},\\ &\mathcal{E}_{(1 - R\delta,U\delta),C} := \left\{ \sigma_{(1 - R\delta,L\delta),C} :=C \left[\frac{1}{2} \ket{0}\!\bra{0} \otimes \rho_{1 - R\delta} + \frac{1}{2} \ket{1}\!\bra{1} \otimes \rho_{L\delta} \right] C^{\dagger}\right\}_{\rho_{\varepsilon} \sim \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}}. \end{align}

This construction ensures that the average purity of \mathcal{E}_{(1,0)} and \mathcal{E}_{(1 - R\delta,L\delta)} equals each others, as manifest below: \begin{align} &\mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{(1,0),C}} \mathrm{tr}\left(\rho^{2}\right) = 1/4 + (1/4) \cdot (1/2^{n-1}) = \frac{1}{4}\left(1+\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\right), \\ &\mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{(1 - R\delta,U\delta),C}} \mathrm{tr}\left(\rho^{2}\right) = \frac{1}{4}\frac{2^{n-1}(1 - R\delta) + 1}{2^{n-1} + 1 - R\delta} + \frac{1}{4}\frac{2^{n-1} L\delta + 1}{2^{n-1} + L\delta} = \frac{1}{4}(1 - \delta) + \frac{1}{4}(\frac{1}{2^{n-1}} + \delta) = \frac{1}{4}\left(1+\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\right). \end{align} We now build uniform distribution on all n-qubit Clifford gates \mathcal{D}. Since Clifford gate forms a 2-design, we can directly write the average based on the value of average purity \begin{align} &\rho_0 := \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{(1,0),C\sim \mathcal{D}}} \rho^{\otimes 2}=\mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{(1 - R\delta,U\delta),C\sim \mathcal{D}}} \rho^{\otimes 2} = a\cdot \mathbb{I}_{2n}/2^{2n} + b\cdot \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}/2^{n}, \\ & a + b = 1, \quad 2^{-n} a + 2^{n} b = \text{Avg. Purity} = 4^{-1}(1 + 2^{-n+1}). \end{align} Solve the equation for a and b, we get the result: \begin{align} \rho_0 = (1 - \mu) \frac{\mathbb{I}_n^{\otimes 2}}{2^{2n}} + \mu \frac{\mathbb{I}_n^{\otimes 2} + \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}}{2^n(2^{n} + 1)}, \text{~where~} \mu = 4^{-1} \frac{2^n -2}{2^n - 1}. \end{align} This prevents the Lemma [lemma:hard_necess1] giving an efficient 2-replica strategy that discriminates \mathcal{E}_{(1,0),C} and \mathcal{E}_{(1 - R\delta,U\delta),C}. However, given a fixed C \in \mathcal{C}, the average of \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^2) for P = C^\dagger Z_1 C has a constant gap \delta/2: \begin{align} &\mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{(1,0),C}} \mathrm{tr}\left(P\rho^{2}\right) = 1/4 - (1/4) \cdot (1/2^{n-1}) = \frac{1}{4}\left(1- \frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\right) ,\\ &\mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{(1 - R\delta,U\delta),C}} \mathrm{tr}\left(P\rho^{2}\right) = \frac{1}{4}(1 - \delta) - \frac{1}{4}(\frac{1}{2^{n-1}} + \delta) = \frac{1}{4}\left(1- \frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\right) - \frac{\delta}{2}. \end{align} This means that if one can use strategy \mathcal{A} to estimate \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^2), \forall P \in \{C^\dagger Z_1 C\}_{C \in \mathcal{C}} within additive error \delta/4, he can use \mathcal{A} to discriminate \mathcal{E}_{(1,0),C} and \mathcal{E}_{(1 - R\delta,U\delta),C}, as rigorously proved below:

重要Lemma

An algorithm that estimates \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^2), \forall P \in \{C Z_1 C^\dagger\}_{C \in \mathcal{C}} can be used to distinguish \mathcal{E}_{(1,0),C} from \mathcal{E}_{(1 - R\delta,U\delta),C} for arbitrary distribution on \mathcal{C}.

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. ◻

Now we prove that two-replica strategy that discriminate \sigma_{(1,0),C}^{\otimes 2} from \sigma_{(1 - R\delta,L\delta),C}^{\otimes 2} require \Omega(2^{n}) rounds. Given a T-round 2-replica measurement strategy M_s = \bigotimes_{t = 1}^{T} F_{s_t}^{u_t}, where \{F_{s}^{u}\}_{s} is a POVM on space \mathcal{H}(d^2). Now the TVD under this measurement takes the value: \begin{align} \delta_{\mathrm{tvd}} = \left|\mathrm{tr}\left(M_s \mathbb{E}_{C}C^{\otimes 2T}\mathbb{E}_{\psi}\left(\sigma_{(1,0),I}^{\otimes 2T} - \sigma_{(1 - R\delta,L\delta),I}^{\otimes 2T}\right)(C^\dagger)^{\otimes 2T}\right)\right|, \end{align} where the Haar average takes the value: \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\psi}\sigma_{(1,0),I}^{\otimes 2T} &= \left[\frac{1}{2}\ket{0}\!\bra{0} \otimes \psi + \frac{1}{2}\ket{1}\!\bra{1} \otimes 2^{-n+1}\mathbb{I}_{n-1}\right]^{\otimes 2T} = \sum_{\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2T}} \frac{2^{-2T}\ket{\bar{\mathbf{a}}}\!\bra{\bar{\mathbf{a}}} }{d^{\uparrow |\mathbf{a}|} d^{2T - |\mathbf{a}|}}\otimes\sum_{\pi \in S_{2T}^{\mathbf{a}}} \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{d},\\ \mathbb{E}_{\psi}\sigma_{(1 - R\delta,L\delta),I}^{\otimes 2T} &= \left[\frac{1}{2}\ket{0}\!\bra{0} \otimes \rho_{1 - R\delta} + \frac{1}{2}\ket{1}\!\bra{1} \otimes 2^{-n+1}\rho_{L\delta}\right]^{\otimes 2T} \\ &= \sum_{\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2T}} {2^{-2T}\ket{\bar{\mathbf{a}}}\!\bra{\bar{\mathbf{a}}}} \otimes \frac{\sum_{\pi \in S_{2T}^{\mathbf{a}}, \sigma \in S_{2T}^{\bar{\mathbf{a}}}} \mathbb{P}_{\pi \sigma}^{d} (1 - R \delta)^{-c(\pi)} (L\delta)^{-c(\sigma)}}{[d/(1 - R\delta)]^{\uparrow |\mathbf{a}|} [d/L\delta]^{\uparrow |\bar{\mathbf{a}}|}}, \end{align} where d = 2^{n-1} and S_{2T}^{\mathbf{a}} denoting the permutation contained in position \{i|a_i = 1\}. If we defined the operator \mathbb{S}^{\mathbf{a}} = \sum_{\pi \in S_{2T}^{\mathbf{a}}} \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{d} and D = 2d = 2^n, we conclude that \begin{align} \Phi_{\mathrm{U},2T}\left[ \ket{{\mathbf{a}}}\!\bra{{\mathbf{a}}}\otimes\mathbb{S}^{\mathbf{a}}\right] = \sum_{\rho \sigma \in S_{2T}} \mathrm{Wg}_{\rho\sigma}^{D} \mathrm{tr}\left[\ket{{\mathbf{a}}}\!\bra{{\mathbf{a}}}\otimes\mathbb{S}^{\mathbf{a}} \cdot \mathrm{SWAP}_{\sigma} \otimes \mathbb{P}_{\sigma}^{d}\right] \mathbb{P}_{\rho}^{D}. \end{align} The trace term can be explicitly calcluated as \begin{align} &\mathrm{tr}\left[\ket{{\mathbf{a}}}\!\bra{{\mathbf{a}}}\otimes\mathbb{S}^{\mathbf{a}} \cdot \mathrm{SWAP}_{\sigma} \otimes \mathbb{P}_{\sigma}^{d}\right]= \delta_{\mathbf{a}, \sigma{\mathbf{a}}} \sum_{\pi \in S_{2T}^{\mathbf{a}}} \mathrm{tr}\left(\mathbb{P}_{\pi \sigma}^{d}\right) = \delta_{\sigma, \beta \gamma} \sum_{\pi \in S_{2T}^{{\mathbf{a}}}} d^{c(\pi\gamma)} = \delta_{\sigma, \beta \gamma} \frac{d^{\uparrow |\mathbf{a}|}}{d^{|{\mathbf{a}}|}}d^{c(\gamma)}. \end{align} Here in the second equality we use the fact that \mathbf{a} = \sigma(\mathbf{a}) if and only if \sigma = \beta \cdot \gamma for \beta\in S_{2T}^{\mathbf{a}} and \gamma \in S_{2T}^{\bar{\mathbf{a}}}. In the last equality, we use the identity \begin{align} \forall \gamma \in S_{2T}^{\bar{\mathbf{a}}}, \sum_{\pi\in S_{2T}^{\mathbf{a}}} d^{c(\pi\gamma )} = \frac{d^{\uparrow |\mathbf{a}|}}{d^{|{\mathbf{a}}|}}d^{c(\gamma)} \end{align} Noted that the unitary average of \sum_{\mathbf{a}}2^{-2T}\ket{{\mathbf{a}}}\!\bra{{\mathbf{a}}} \otimes \rho_{\mathbf{a}} and \sum_{\mathbf{a}}2^{-2T}\ket{\bar{\mathbf{a}}}\!\bra{\bar{\mathbf{a}}}\otimes \rho_{\mathbf{a}} are identical since \ket{\mathbf{a}} can be transformed into \ket{\bar{\mathbf{a}}} through 2T-fold unitary X^{2T} and Haar random unitary is shift invariant. Thus, the average state \rho_0 is the linear combination of permutation operators: \begin{align} &\Phi_{\mathrm{U},2T}\left[ \mathbb{E}_{\psi}\sigma_{(1,0),I}^{\otimes 2T} \right] = \Phi_{\mathrm{U},2T}\left[ \mathbb{E}_{\psi}\sigma_{(0,1),I}^{\otimes 2T} \right] :=\rho_0 = \Phi_{\mathrm{U},2T}\left[ \sum_{\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2T}}\frac{ \ket{{\mathbf{a}}}\!\bra{{\mathbf{a}}}\otimes\mathbb{S}^{\mathbf{a}}}{2^{2T}d^{\uparrow |\mathbf{a}|} d^{2T - |\mathbf{a}|}}\right]\\ & = \sum_{\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2T}}\sum_{\sigma,\rho \in S_{2T}}\frac{\mathrm{Wg}_{\rho \sigma}^{D}\cdot \delta_{\sigma,\beta\gamma}\frac{d^{\uparrow |\mathbf{a}|}}{d^{|{\mathbf{a}}|}}d^{c(\gamma)}}{2^{2T}d^{\uparrow |\mathbf{a}|} d^{2T - |\mathbf{a}|}} \mathbb{P}_{\rho}^{D} =\sum_{\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2T}}\sum_{\rho \in S_{2T}}\sum_{\beta \in S_{2T}^{{\mathbf{a}}},\gamma\in S_{2T}^{\bar{\mathbf{a}}}}\frac{\mathrm{Wg}_{\rho(\beta\gamma)}^{D}\cdot d^{c(\gamma)}}{2^{2T} d^{2T}} \mathbb{P}_{\rho}^{D} \end{align} Similarly, we calculate \begin{align} &\mathrm{tr}\left[\left(\ket{\bar{\mathbf{a}}}\!\bra{\bar{\mathbf{a}}}\otimes \frac{\sum_{\pi \in S_{2T}^{\mathbf{a}}, \nu \in S_{2T}^{\bar{\mathbf{a}}}} \mathbb{P}_{\pi \nu}^{d} (1 - R \delta)^{-c(\pi)} (L\delta)^{-c(\nu)}}{[d/(1 - R\delta)]^{\uparrow |\mathbf{a}|} [d/L\delta]^{\uparrow |\bar{\mathbf{a}}|}}\right)\cdot \mathrm{SWAP}_{\sigma} \otimes \mathbb{P}_{\sigma}^{d}\right]\\ &= \delta_{\sigma, \beta\gamma}\sum_{\pi \in S_{2T}^{\mathbf{a}}, \nu \in S_{2T}^{\bar{\mathbf{a}}}}\frac{ d^{c(\pi \nu)} (1 - R \delta)^{-c(\pi \beta^{-1})} (L\delta)^{-c(\nu\gamma^{-1})}}{[d/(1 - R\delta)]^{\uparrow |\mathbf{a}|} [d/L\delta]^{\uparrow |\bar{\mathbf{a}}|}}. \end{align} When \delta = 0, this expression reduced to \delta_{\sigma,\beta\gamma}d^{-2T} d^{c(\gamma)}. R \delta)^{-c(\pi \beta^{-1})} (L\delta)^{-c(\nu\gamma^{-1})}}{2^{2T}[d/(1 - R\delta)]^{\uparrow |\mathbf{a}|} [d/L\delta]^{\uparrow |\bar{\mathbf{a}}|}} \mathbb{P}_{\rho}^{D} \end{align} The difference of two average can then be reform into the discrimination between \mathbb{I}_{n}^{\otimes 2T}/d^{2T} from the mixed state \begin{align} \Phi_{\mathrm{U},2T}\left[ \mathbb{E}_{\psi}\sigma_{(1,0),I}^{\otimes 2T} \right] -\Phi_{\mathrm{U},2T}\left[ \mathbb{E}_{\psi}\sigma_{(1-R\delta,L\delta),I}^{\otimes 2T} \right] = \mathbb{I}_{n}^{\otimes 2T}/D^{2T} + \left[\sum_{\rho \in S_{2T}} \lambda_{\rho} \mathbb{P}_{\rho}^{D} \right] \end{align} This TVD is bounded by the leaves likelihood for M_s = \otimes_{t =1}^{T} F_{s_t}^{u_t} as \begin{align} L(s) = \frac{D^{2T}\mathrm{tr}\left(M_s\left[\sum_{\rho \in S_{2T}} \lambda_{\rho} \mathbb{P}_{\rho}^{D} \right]\right)}{\mathrm{tr}\left(M_s\right)} \geq D^{2T} \prod_{t = 1}^{2T} \frac{\mathrm{tr}\left(F_{s_t}^{u_t}\left[\sum_{\rho \in S_{2}} \lambda'_{\rho} \mathbb{P}_{\rho}^{D} \right]\right)}{\mathrm{tr}\left(F_{s_t}^{u_t}\right)} \end{align} This further reduced the problem to the discrimination between \mathbb{I}(D)^{\otimes 2}/D^2 and \sum_{\rho \in S_{2}} \lambda'_{\rho} \mathbb{P}_{\rho}^{D} Based on Lemma [theo:mart_distinguish_lb], we calculate its chi-square divergence first: \begin{align} \delta_{\mathcal{D}} &= \max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}} \sum_{s} \mathrm{tr}\left(\rho_0 F_s\right) \mathbb{E}_{\substack{C \sim \mathcal{D},\psi}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}\left(\sigma_{(1,0),C}^{\otimes 2} F_s\right)}{\mathrm{tr}\left(\rho_0 F_s\right)} - 1\right]^2 = \max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}} \sum_{s} \mathbb{E}_{\substack{C \sim \mathcal{D}, \psi}}\frac{\left\{\mathrm{tr} \left[\left(\sigma_{(1,0),C}^{\otimes 2} - \rho_0\right) F_s\right]\right\}^2}{\mathrm{tr}\left(\rho_0F_s\right)} \notag \\ &\leq (1 - 重要Lemma

An algorithm that estimates \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^2), \forall P \in \{C Z_1 C^\dagger\}_{C \in \mathcal{C}} can be used to distinguish \mathcal{E}_{(2\varepsilon, 0)} from \mathcal{E}_{(\varepsilon, \varepsilon)}.

Proof. However, if we build uniform distribution on all possible Pauli operators, which in turn induces uniform distribution on all n-qubit Clifford gates \mathcal{D}, the operator \mathbb{E}_{C \sim \mathcal{D}} \Delta_2 has exponentially small one-norm, as calculated below: \begin{align} &\mathbb{E}_{C \sim \mathcal{D}} \Delta_2(C) = a \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n} + b \mathbb{I}_{2n}, \text{~with~}\begin{cases} 2^n a + 2^{2n}b = 0.\\ 2^{2n} a + 2^{n}b = \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \cdot \frac{d + 3\varepsilon - \varepsilon d^2}{d(d+\varepsilon)(d + 2 \varepsilon)} . \end{cases} \end{align} Thus, we have a+b,|a-b| \sim \mathcal{O}(2^{-3n}), and \|\mathbb{E}_{C \sim \mathcal{D}} \Delta_2(C)\|_{1} = \mathcal{O}(2^{-n}).

1.6 Symmetric strategies

If there is no restriction on the memory-number and the replica number, we can lower-bound the strategy through the symmetric of the property. We first define general testing strategy rigorously.

注记Definition

A property \mathcal{P} \subset \mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H}) is a set of quantum states. A two-outcome POVM \{E,\mathbb{I} - E\} on k-copies of n-qubit states tests the property \mathcal{P} iff for certain 1>\varepsilon_B \geq \varepsilon_A >0 and \delta = \Theta(1), \begin{align} d_{\text{tr}}(\rho, \mathcal{P}) \leq \varepsilon_A \Rightarrow \text{tr}(E \rho^{\otimes k}) \geq 1/2 +\delta,\\ d_{\text{tr}}(\rho, \mathcal{P}) \geq \varepsilon_B \Rightarrow \text{tr}(E \rho^{\otimes k}) \leq 1/2 - \delta. \end{align}

Now suppose the testing property \mathcal{P}, which is a set of state within n-qubit space, is invariant under unitary operation U(G) , which is a subgroup of U(2)^{\otimes n}. Namely, \begin{align} \forall \sigma \in \mathcal{P},\forall V \in U(G), V\sigma V^\dagger \in \mathcal{P}. \end{align} Then we are prepared to show that it is enough to consider the symmetric version of the strategy rather than an arbitrary POVM within n-qubit space, as stated by Lemma [lemma:symmtric_M] below

重要Lemma

Given a k-replica strategy \{E, \mathbb{I } - E\} for the U(G)-symmetric property \mathcal{P} on n-qubits, the symmetric strategy \{\Phi(E), \mathbb{I } - \Phi(E)\} with \Phi(E) := |U(G)|^{-1}\sum_{V \in U(G)} V^{\dagger,\otimes k}EV^{\otimes k} and \Phi_k(E) := |S_k|^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_k} \text{SWAP}_\pi E\cdot\text{SWAP}_\pi has non-decreasing efficiency.

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. Because the unitary invariant property of \mathcal{P} and the non-decreasing property of trace distance under unitary transformation d_{\text{tr}}(\cdot,\cdot) = d_{\text{tr}}(U\cdot U^\dagger,U\cdot U^\dagger), we conclude that \begin{align} d_{\text{tr}}(\rho, \mathcal{P}) \leq \varepsilon_A &\Rightarrow \forall U \in U(G), d_{\text{tr}}(U\rho U^\dagger, \mathcal{P}) \leq \varepsilon_A \\ &\Rightarrow \forall U \in U(G),\text{tr}( EU^{\otimes k}\rho^{\otimes k} U^{\dagger,\otimes k}) \geq 1/2 + \Theta(1),\\ &\Leftrightarrow \forall U \in U(G),|U(G)|^{-1}\sum_{V \in U(G)}\text{tr}(U^{\dagger,\otimes k} EU^{\otimes k}\rho^{\otimes k} ) \geq 1/2 + \Theta(1),\\ &\Leftrightarrow \forall U \in U(G),\text{tr}(\bar E\rho^{\otimes k} ) \geq 1/2 + \Theta(1) \end{align} Similarly, we can prove that d_{\text{tr}}(\rho, \mathcal{P}) \geq \varepsilon_B \Rightarrow \text{tr}(\bar E \rho^{\otimes k}) \leq 1/2 - \Theta(1). The same procedure is applied for \bar{E} := |S_k|^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_k} \text{SWAP}_\pi E\cdot\text{SWAP}_\pi. Thus, we prove that the symmetric strategy \{\bar{E}, \mathbb{I } - \bar{E}\} will have at least the same testing efficiency. ◻

Then we discuss the symmetry for the estimation problem.

注记Definition

A quantitative property of states is a map f: \rho \to \mathbb{R} with \rho \in \mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H}) . Given a POVM \{M_m\}_{m \in R} on k-replica space, an k-replica estimator of f is an observable O \in \text{End}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k}) such that \text{tr}(O \rho^{\otimes k}) = f(\rho). An estimator O is efficient k-replica strategy iff \text{Var}_{\rho^{\otimes k}}(O)\leq \text{Var}_{\rho^{\otimes k}}(O') for all O \in \text{End}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k}).

We say a quantitative property f is invariant under unitary operation U(G) iff f(U\cdot U^\dagger) = f(\cdot), \forall U \in U(G). The we gives the symmetric strategy for estimate problem.

重要Lemma

If O is a k-replica estimator for property f. Then the symmetrized estimators \begin{align} \Phi(O):= |U(G)|^{-1}\sum_{V \in U(G)} V^{\dagger,\otimes k}OV^{\otimes k},\Phi_{k}(O):= |S_k|^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_k} \mathbb{P}_\pi^{d,\dagger} \cdot O\cdot \mathbb{P}_\pi^{d}, \end{align} always satisfied \text{Var}_{\rho^{\otimes k}}(\Phi(O))\leq \text{Var}_{\rho^{\otimes k}}(O),\text{Var}_{\rho^{\otimes k}}(\Phi_k(O))\leq \text{Var}_{\rho^{\otimes k}}(O).

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. We will show a more general statement for arbitrary channel that is unital (\Phi(\mathbb{I}) = \mathbb{I}), positive (\forall \rho \succeq 0, \Phi(\rho) \succeq 0), and satisfied \forall O \in \text{Herm}(\mathcal{H}), \text{tr}(\rho \Phi(O)) = \text{tr}(\rho O). By definition, \text{Var}_{\rho}(\Phi(O)) = \text{tr}(\rho \Phi(O)^2) - \text{tr}^2(\rho \Phi(O)) = [\text{tr}(\rho \Phi(O)^2) - \text{tr}(\rho O^2)]+ \text{Var}_{\rho}(O). According to Theorem [theo:KS_ineq], \Phi(O^2)-\Phi(O)^2\succeq 0, which shows that \text{tr}(\rho \Phi(O)^2)<\text{tr}(\rho \Phi(O^2)) = \text{tr}(\rho O^2). This directly gives the result \text{Var}_{\rho}(\Phi(O)) \leq \text{Var}_{\rho}(O). ◻

Thanks to the Lemma [lemma:symmtric_M] and Lemma [lemma:symmetric_O] , if we find the lower bound of the sample complexity of all the symmetric POVM and operators, any strategy’s sample complexity is lower bounded by this value.

1.6.1 The unitary case U(G) = U(2^n)

The simplest case are properties that is invariant under a unitary transformation. The lemma [lemma:symmtric_M] is useful because any spectrum testing strategy \{M,\mathbb{I} - M\} now can be restated as weak Schur sampling followed by classical post-processing  [2], as stated by the theorem below.

重要Lemma

Given a testing strategy \{M, \mathbb{I } - M\} for unitary invariant property \mathcal{P} such that: \begin{align} \tr(M \rho^{\otimes k}) &\geq 1 - \delta,\forall \rho \in \mathcal{P};\\ \tr(M \rho^{\otimes k}) &\leq 1 - f(\varepsilon),\forall \rho ~\varepsilon \text{-far from~} \mathcal{P}. \end{align} Another strategy \bar{M} such that [\bar M,U^{\otimes k}] =0 and [\bar M,\text{SWAP}_\pi]=0 can be constructed with non-decreasing efficiency.

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. M_s =|S_k|^{-1} \sum_{\pi \in S^k}\mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{2^n}\cdot M \cdot\mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{2^n} have unchanged efficiency because \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{2^n}\cdot \rho^{\otimes k} \cdot\mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{2^n} = \rho^{\otimes k}. Combined with lemma [lemma:symmtric_M] proves the result. ◻

This construction simplified the analysis because we can reduce arbitrary strategy to a canonical one-weak Shur sampling. To see this, we first cite the lemma in  [3], according to the famous Schur-Weyl duality.

重要Lemma

Given the symmetry group S_k , use \kappa \vdash k labels the conjugate classes K(\kappa) and \lambda \vdash k label the irreducible representation with the character function \chi_{\lambda}(\cdot) and dimension \text{dim}~\lambda. Define the projective measurements P_\lambda and the conjugate-class observables O_{\kappa} as \begin{align} P_{\lambda} := (\text{dim}\lambda)({k!})^{-1} \sum_{\pi \in S_k} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) \mathbb{P}_\pi^d,\quad O_{\kappa} := |K(\kappa)|^{-1} \sum_{\pi \in K(\kappa)} \mathbb{P}_\pi^d. \end{align} If \forall U \in \mathbb{C}^{k} and \forall \pi \in S_k, the operator M on the space (\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes k} satisfies [M,U^{\otimes k}] =0 and [M,\mathbb{P}_\pi^d]=0, then M can be decomposed as \begin{align} M &= \sum_{\lambda \vdash k} \alpha_{\lambda} P_\lambda,\quad M = \sum_{\kappa \vdash k} \beta_{\kappa} O_\kappa, \label{eq:M_decomp} \\ &\text{where~}O_{\kappa} = \sum_{\lambda}{(\text{dim}\lambda)^{-1}}\chi_{\lambda}(\kappa) P_{\lambda}. \label{eq:relation_PM} \end{align}

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. The proof of this theorem is separated into three steps. First, by Schur-Weyl duality, we know that [M,U^{\otimes k}]=0 iff M is a linear superposition of SWAP gates: \begin{align} \label{eq:M_decomp_mid} M &= \sum_{g \in S_k} f(g) \cdot \text{SWAP}_g. \end{align}

Then we show that linear combination of SWAP gates commute with all the SWAP gates iff the superposition coefficient is a class function. According to Eq. [eq:M_decomp_mid], M is the image of group algebra m = \sum_{g \in S_k} f(g) g under representation \rho(g) = \text{SWAP}_g. Then m must commute with arbitray element in S_k. \forall~ h \in S_k, notice that: \begin{align} hmh^{-1} &= \sum_{g \in S_k} f(g) \cdot{hgh^{-1}} =\sum_{t \in S_k} f(h^{-1} t h) \cdot{t} =\sum_{g \in S_k} f(g) \cdot g = m \end{align} This then imply f(g) = f(h^{-1} t h) for all h \in S_k and f is a class function. Last, given that character functions forms a orthonormal basis for class function, we obtain f(g) = \sum_{\lambda}c_{\lambda} \chi_{\lambda}(g). Plug into Eq. [eq:M_decomp_mid] gives: \begin{align} M &= \sum_{\lambda}c_{\lambda} \sum_{g \in S_k}\chi_{\lambda}(g)\cdot \text{SWAP}_g =\sum_{\lambda} \alpha_{\lambda} \frac{\text{dim}(V_\lambda)}{k!} \sum_{\pi \in S_k} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) \text{SWAP}_\pi = \sum_{\lambda} \alpha_{\lambda} P_\lambda \end{align} This is indeed a projector based on Lemma [lemma:projector_in_lambda] proved before. To prove the conclusion (ii), we first noted that \begin{align} \sum_{\lambda}\frac{1}{\text{dim~}\lambda}\chi_{\lambda}(\kappa) P_{\lambda} &= \sum_{\pi \in S_k} ({k!})^{-1}\sum_{\lambda}\chi_{\lambda}(\kappa) \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) \mathbb{P}^d_\pi\\ &=|K(\kappa)|^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in K(\kappa)} \mathbb{P}^d_\pi = O_{\kappa} \end{align} Here in the second line we use the second orthogonal identity |G|^{-1}\sum_{p}\chi_{p}(\kappa_j)\chi_{p}(\kappa_k) = |K(\kappa_k)|^{-1}\delta_{jk}. Then plug in Eq. [eq:M_decomp] we get \begin{align} \sum_{\kappa \vdash k} \beta_{\kappa} O_\kappa =\sum_{\lambda\vdash k}\frac{1}{\text{dim}~\lambda}\left[ \sum_{\kappa \vdash k} \beta_{\kappa} \chi_{\lambda}(\kappa)\right] P_{\lambda}= \sum_{\lambda \vdash k} \alpha_{\lambda} P_\lambda. \end{align} This implys the transformation (\text{dim}\lambda)\cdot \alpha_{\lambda} = \sum_{\kappa \vdash k} \beta_{\kappa} \chi_{\lambda}(\kappa). ◻

1.6.2 Examples.

When k = 2, the group S_2 only has two conjugate class (2,0) and (1,1). The corresponding projectors are P_{(2,0)} = 2^{-1}{(\mathbb{I} + \text{SWAP}_{(1,2)})},P_{(1,1)} = 2^{-1}{(\mathbb{I} - \text{SWAP}_{(1,2)})}. This is just the SWAP test of two identical states, which is widely used for purity test. For larger t, the computation of those exact projector is proved to be #P-hard  [4]. Fortunately, the realization of projective measurement \{P_\lambda\} can be implemented in time \text{Poly}(k,\ln d) with generalized phase estimation circuit  [5], which is efficient for n-qubits property testing with d = 2^n. This is called the weak Schur sampling (WSS). Now we characterize the result of WSS by polynomials of density matrix’s spectrum.

注记Definition

Let \mu,\lambda\vdash k be a partition of the replica number k. Let \mathcal{T} be the set of all semi-standard Young tableaus with shape \lambda and alphabet \{1,\cdots,d\}. Let \#(T,i) be the number of times that the character i occurs in the semi-standard Young tableau T. Two rank-k symmetric polynomials of d variables \mathbf{x}=(x_1,\cdots,x_d) can be defined below.

  • Schur polynomial (SP) is a rank-k symmetric polynomial that s_{\lambda}(\mathbf x):= \sum_{T}\prod_{i=1}^d x_i^{\#(T,i)}

  • Power sum polynomial (PSP) is a rank-k symmetric polynomial that M_{\mu}(\mathbf{x}):=\prod_{i=1}^{l(\mu)} \sum_{j=1}^d x_j^{\mu_i}

1.6.3 Examples.

If we take \lambda = (k,0,\cdots), we get the \sum_{j = 1}^d x_j^k. SP and PSP can decompose each other, as shown in Lemma [lemma:sym_poly_decomp] below.

重要Lemma

Any rank-k power sum polynomial can be decomposed with the rank-k symmetric Schur polynomial through M_{\mu}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{\lambda \vdash k}\chi_{\lambda}(\mu)s_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}).

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. ◻

Refer to  [6], the distribution of \text{tr}(P_{\lambda} \rho^{\otimes k}) only relates to the spectrum \eta of \rho, as proved in Lemma [lemma:WSS_res] below. Thus, we use \text{SW}_{\rho}^k(\lambda) to denote the weak Schur sampling probability \text{tr}(P_\lambda \rho^{\otimes k}) where \lambda is the eigenvalue of the density matrix \rho.

重要Lemma

Defined \text{dim}(\lambda) as the number of standard Young tableaus of shape \lambda \vdash k and alphabet [k]. Then \text{SW}_{\rho}^k(\lambda)= \text{dim}(\lambda) \cdot s_\lambda (\eta_1,\cdots,\eta_d) with \eta the spectrum of \rho. Specifically, we have \text{SW}_{d^{-1}\mathbb{I}}^k(\lambda) = {(\text{dim} (\lambda))^2}{(k!)^{-1}} {d^{\uparrow \lambda}}({d^k})^{-1}, where denots d^{\uparrow \lambda}: = \prod_{(i,j) \in [\lambda]} (d + j - i) with i,j labeling the position of all the lattices in Young tableaus of shape \lambda \vdash n,

注记Proof (Click to expand)

Proof. \begin{align} \label{eq:Schur_prob} \text{tr}(P_\lambda \rho^{\otimes k}) = (\text{dim}\lambda)({k!})^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in S_k} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) \text{tr}( \text{SWAP}_\pi \rho^{\otimes k}). \end{align} If \pi has l cycles with cycle length \kappa_1\cdots\kappa_l and \rho has eigenvalues \eta_1,\cdots,\eta_{d}, we noted that \begin{align} \text{tr}( \text{SWAP}_\pi \rho^{\otimes k}) = \text{tr}(\rho^{\kappa_1})\times \cdots\times\text{tr}(\rho^{\kappa_l}) = M_{\kappa}(\eta). \end{align} Plug into Eq. [eq:Schur_prob] gives \begin{align} \text{tr}(P_\lambda \rho^{\otimes k}) &= (\text{dim}\lambda)({k!})^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in S_k} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) M_{\kappa}(\eta)\\ &=(\text{dim}\lambda)({k!})^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in S_k} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) \sum_{\omega \vdash k}\chi_{\omega}(\pi)s_{\omega}(\eta)\\ &=(\text{dim}\lambda) \cdot s_{\lambda}(\eta). \end{align} Here in the second equality, we use Lemma [lemma:sym_poly_decomp]. In the third equality, we use the orthorgonal equation of group characters |G|^{-1} \sum_{g \in G} \chi_{p}^*(g)\chi_{q}(g) = \delta_{pq}. ◻
